#2833. Tech outages are causing people to panic-buy. Costco is benefiting, Mizuho says

A series of tech outages has consumers stocking up on emergency supplies.

Costco sales are seeing a lift because of it, according to research firm Mizuho.

In the final week of October, Mizuho estimates, Costco's U.S. comparable sales, excluding gasoline, rose 11% to 12%, up from the normal 6% to 7% the first three weeks in October. Costco reported an 8.1% increase for the month. The firm said the stronger pace is continuing through November, as 21 of the 26 high-ticket generators it tracked on Costco's website sold out as of Sunday night.

Shares of Costco were roughly flat-to-lower in Wednesday morning trading at around $1,107 apiece.

"Consumer anxiety following the Microsoft Outlook outage, the ground stoppage for all U.S. airline flights, and apocalyptic concerns flaring up across social media have all contributed to increased emergency prep sales at COST," Mizuho analyst David Bellinger said in a research note Monday. Bellinger will appear on CNBC's "The Exchange" during the 1 p.m. hour.

On Thursday, an outage occurred in Microsoft's Outlook and Teams, and on Friday the Federal Aviation Administration halted departures nationwide. On Monday, a software outage at JPMorgan Chase caused banking transaction delays, and a system outage delayed United Airlines flights. The National Security Agency said Tuesday that the spy agency's communication network went down temporarily.

The outages appear to come amid a rush to recover software vulnerabilities uncovered by AI tools, and officials are saying there's no reason for panic.

Still, on TikTok and other social media platforms, posts urging people to stock up on food and supplies are gaining significant traction.

Mizuho raised its price target on Costco to $1,150 from $1,100 and kept its buy-equivalent outperform rating. The firm said U.S. comparable sales could grow more than 10% in November.

Mizuho also sees Walmart's Sam's Club benefiting from emergency preparedness sales as shoppers fill up their pantries, and for Home Depot and Lowe's as they buy home improvement emergency supplies.

At Costco, Mizuho will be watching whether the surge brought in new member sign-ups when the warehouse retailer reports its first quarter of fiscal 2027 on Dec. 10.

#2832. Zach LaVine, Kings hope Darius Acuff Jr. won't be negatively impacted by losing

Zach LaVine, Kings hope Darius Acuff Jr. won't be negatively impacted by losing originally appeared on NBC Sports Bay Area

SACRAMENTO – Zach LaVine has no illusions about what this season is about for the Kings.

The veteran guard, who became Sacramento's oldest player during the offseason, likely will be playing elsewhere after his massive $215 million contract expires this summer.

But despite that, the 31-year-old has maintained perspective that his team's season is all about rookie point guard Darius Acuff Jr. and the team's other impressionable young players that are going through a historically bad stretch to begin the season.

"We just don't want to let the younger dudes hang their head and get into these rhythms of, OK, this is OK and this is how we're going (to do this). It's bad," LaVine said Wednesday. "And that's not a way that you want to start your career or have that type of intensity. I think some of those dudes are keeping everybody positive in the gym, working for the next thing."

LaVine was the first member of the Kings to the postgame podium after Sacramento lost to the Phoenix Suns, 128-107, falling to 1-13 on the 2026-27 NBA season and tying the 1990-91 team for the worst start in franchise history.

Worse yet, the Kings dropped to 0-9 at home. Losing to Phoenix meant Sacramento lost every game of its seven-game home stand, the longest of the season.

And things won't get any easier. They travel to Los Angeles to take on the 13-3 Lakers on Friday before hosting the 11-4 Boston Celtics at Golden 1 Center on Saturday. The next five games are all against teams with winning records before the Kings welcome the struggling New Orleans Pelicans on Nov. 30 for the second night of a back-to-back.

"There's not a lot of positive things to say. I got to call a spade a spade. We're 1-13," LaVine said. "But besides us looking at film and looking at the good things we do, the general public isn't going to see that. They're not going to see the hard work or the things that we put into trying to win."

The Kings didn't come into the season thinking they would compete with the elite teams in the Western Conference and make a deep run into the NBA playoffs. They hoped they could be healthier than last season when lengthy absences from LaVine, Domantas Sabonis and Keegan Murray played a role in finishing just 22-60.

They hoped Doug Christie in his second full season would improve as head coach. They hoped Acuff would reinvigorate the franchise after the messy departure of former coach Mike Brown led to the eventual trade of centerpiece De'Aaron Fox in the deal that brought back LaVine.

But none of that has come to fruition, and Acuff's offensive play has been the only bright spot in an otherwise historically bad start to Sacramento's season.

Christie was asked about LaVine's comments and the organization's emphasis on setting the right foundation for Acuff and other young players to build on.

"To be honest, it's everything because that's what we're trying to build here. We're trying to build a sustainable winner," Christie said. "There are parts in what we're doing that are headed the right way. But then all those little things that I'm talking about, those are the things that you got to push aside and you got to stay consistent with it, and you got to make sure you're doing it on a day-to-day basis."

As repetitive as losing has become for the Kings, so has Christie's messaging. He has maintained an upbeat attitude despite all the losing while also admitting he believes he's always on the hot seat.

But it's hard to envision a scenario where Christie remains head coach much longer. The Kings current winning percentage of 0.71 percent would pace out to a 6-76 record, which would be the worst over an 82-game schedule in NBA history.

For Acuff's part, he's saying the right things and trying to maintain a positive attitude.

"You just got to keep high spirits," he said Wednesday after scoring a game-high 36 points, just two shy of his career best. "The key thing is just staying together, making sure we stay together through a tough time. That's the most important part."

#2830. Two new housing reports point to bleak winter ahead, with record low sales

Two new reports on the housing market show activity slowing even more, after a September spike in mortgage rates sent it into a deep freeze.

Pending home sales in October dropped 4.7% month-over-month and were down 16.7% from October of last year, according to the National Association of Realtors. This is the lowest level in the index's 25-year history.

Analysts had been looking for a much smaller decline, likely because mortgage rates pulled back slightly in October, only to rise sharply again last week. The average rate on the 30-year fixed started October at 7.54% according to Mortgage News Daily and ended the month at 7.27%.

The pending count is based on signed contracts — people out shopping and signing deals during the month. It is therefore an indicator of future closed sales.

"Two consecutive months of record-low pending contracts point to very sluggish fourth-quarter home sales closings, and annual existing-home sales could be the lowest since the mid-1990s," said Lawrence Yun, NAR's chief economist in a release.

Regionally, sales were down across the nation with the sharpest drops in the South, which is usually busiest for sales and the West which is most expensive.

Another report released Wednesday showed gains in home construction in October but raised a red flag going forward. Single-family housing starts rose 4% from September, according to the U.S. Census, but were down 3.2% year over year. Building permits, an indicator of future construction, dropped 8.7% for the month and were down 12.9% from October 2025. That is the lowest level for permits since May 2020, the start of the Covid-19 pandemic.

"Builders are dealing with a litany of obstacles to selling homes, whether it's rising costs of land, labor, and materials, high financing costs, or weak buyer demand," wrote Joel Berner, senior economist at Realtor.com. "This month's data shows them slowing down activity at the top of their funnel, which will result in slower months of starts and completions later on."

The construction report follows a bleak reading on homebuilder sentiment, which fell to the lowest level in 14 years in November, on the monthly index from the National Association of Home Builders. Builders cited multiple challenges, including higher mortgage rates, higher costs for energy, materials and labor, as well as weaker consumer confidence.

#2829. Tennis the saviour for player who tried to take own life before Wimbledon

Warning: This article contains references to suicide

The clues were there. Leandro Riedi struggled to even force a smile after winning a match which moved him closer to the Wimbledon main draw.

These are the moments usually cherished and celebrated by a player ranked outside of the world's top 100.

The Swiss player's solemn reaction was jarring, but then nobody outside of his immediate circle knew what had happened a few days earlier.

Shortly before Wimbledon qualifying began in June 2024, Riedi had tried to take his own life.

Panic attacks had been plaguing the world number 137 for almost 18 months. Anxiety and self-doubt had been around for much longer.

The toll they were taking on his mental health meant he felt there was no other way out.

"I always had anxiety. I was always a shy person, especially when I was younger. I always had this mindset that I wasn't good enough," Riedi told BBC Sport.

"I always thought I needed to do something special. I have to be perfect. This was my mental battle all the time.

"February 2023 to November 2024 was a horrible period of time. I was always scared of having a panic attack. I had no control over it whatsoever."

Very few people knew the extent of Riedi's mental health issues until he revealed last week that he had attempted suicide.

The 24-year-old wants to make two things clear.

Firstly, he is not looking for sympathy. He has only decided to talk about his experience to "send a strong message" for others struggling with their mental health.

Secondly, he is now in a "very good" place, thanks to professional treatment he has received over the past two years.

"I hope nobody ever has to go through what I did - it's horrifying and scary," Riedi said.

"But I want to be an example it can turn out well."

In his darkest moments Riedi found salvation in the sport which he started playing as a three-year-old growing up in Zurich.

"I felt really home at a tennis court - I was able to perform and I was able to play," he said.

"So tennis was my saviour in that time. It helped me to go out of my thoughts for one second and focus on doing what I love."

It goes some way to explaining why Riedi decided to still compete at Wimbledon so soon after attempting to end his life.

Looking back, he is unsure how he summoned the strength to play.

"My coach told me to go home. He was the only one who knew. But then what? Be sad at home?" Riedi said.

"I didn't want to go home. I wanted to stay and I wanted to play. It was a horrible, horrible week.

"After the first round I remember I just left and went to the hotel. Usually you're excited and happy about a win, but I couldn't speak."

In his hotel room Riedi continued to have troubled thoughts.

He credits his psychologist, who stayed awake with Riedi until 3am to make sure he was not alone, for saving his life.

Riedi went on to win his second qualifying match before losing in the third and final round. At first he felt the pressure was "lifted", but not competing created a void.

Riedi describes how he was "scared" to leave his hotel room for the next two weeks, only going out to collect food deliveries from the lobby.

Tennis continued to be the only force which Riedi thought provided purpose. He managed to leave London for a tournament in Sweden, banking on it "bringing happiness".

But, after winning a match in Gstaad, he started to realise that going on to court was merely a placebo effect.

The catalyst of change came a few weeks later when a knee injury - the first "big injury" of his career - required surgery following the US Open.

"It was devastating for me because I knew my one happiness - tennis - was gone," Riedi said.

"In tennis I always had to fight [my mental health] because I was still playing. I didn't want to show any weakness.

"Then I realised I didn't want to fight any more. I wanted to help it. I wanted to work with it."

Riedi (right) reached the Surbiton Challenger final just before Wimbledon qualifying in 2024, finishing runner-up to South Africa's Lloyd Harris (left) [Getty Images]

Focusing on tennis and receiving the support of his "closest people" helped Riedi through his most troubled times.

Reopening his psychological "wounds", and discussing his inner trauma with experts, has been the key to his recovery.

He no longer has suicidal thoughts. The panic attacks have stopped. He still has anxiety but possesses the coping mechanisms to prevent it being debilitating.

Riedi had been planning to open up publicly for several months. He still felt nervous when he hit publish on his social media post, but he has been heartened by an overwhelmingly warm response.

"I have got messages from all over the world. Someone texted me from India saying they saw the post and are going through something similar right now," Riedi said.

"They said 'Your message really helped me. It gave me some power to believe it's going to work.' That's exactly what I was aiming for.

"People think tennis pros have all they need. I wanted to showcase that it's OK not to be OK even though others think you have everything."

Riedi says his mental health struggles were caused by "private issues" in his life and were not a consequence of his career.

But, with players increasingly speaking out about mental burnout, he wants his words to drive further change.

The ATP already provides an in-house psychology and wellbeing service, which offers confidential support at tournaments and remotely.

If a mental health disorder prevents a player from competing for at least six months, they can apply for a protected ranking. It allows them to enter tournaments without penalty when they are ready to return.

Riedi says the governing bodies can "never do too much", but he thinks there is still an issue on the men's tour with reaching out for support.

"For me, mental health is like a muscle. If your knee is injured, you do surgery and take care of it," he said.

"If you're injured in your mind, it's like you can't speak about it. That's not good.

"I hope my message shows tennis players, or anyone, that speaking out isn't a weakness. It's actually the opposite. It's strong and brave."

Since working on his mental health, Riedi has produced some of the best results of his career.

He came through qualifying to reach the last 16 of the 2025 US Open - his standout performance at a Grand Slam tournament - and climbed to a career-high world ranking of 116 this year.

The most poignant moment came in June 2025 when he returned to Wimbledon.

A year on from his suicide attempt, Riedi decided to stay at the same Chelsea hotel because he wanted "make peace" with what had happened.

"It was very emotional, but in a good way," he said.

"I was like, 'wow, when you really work on something, if you stay consistent about something, one year can do so much'."

This year Riedi's progress on the court has been hampered by a torn tendon in a wrist.

Being sidelined for six months led to some friends wondering why he does not stop playing professionally. He says his "love and passion" for tennis will not allow him.

Riedi says the "sky is still the limit" and plans to make his comeback at the start of 2027, using a protected injury ranking to enter Australian Open qualifying.

"I really had to go through big obstacles, but I'm very proud I did this at such a young age. I'm actually this guy who just likes life," he said.

"I love to do things. I want to be happy. I want to be excited for my future and not be scared."

#2826. Read Jim Cramer’s full interview with Nvidia’s Colette Kress: Demand, buybacks and China

Nvidia delivered another beat-and-raise quarter on Tuesday in the chipmaker's first report since Jensen Huang abruptly resigned as CEO last week amid a widening affair scandal. Revenue more than doubled from a year earlier, exceeding estimates by nearly $7 billion, while earnings topped expectations by 20 cents per share. An excellent quarter by almost any measure.

But investors remain skeptical about Nvidia's future without Huang, who famously founded the company at a San Jose Denny's in 1993. Shares fell 2.5% Wednesday, despite opening higher on the session. Will the company lose its smartest executives and engineers? Would Nvidia remain banker to the increasingly shaky neoclouds? Can it stay ahead of the competition?

On Tuesday night, Colette Kress sat down with CNBC's Jim Cramer shortly after delivering her first earnings call as interim CEO to answer these pressing questions and more.

This transcript has been edited for clarity.

Jim Cramer: After the bell, Nvidia reported earnings, and what a quarter it was. The stock jumped in after hours in response. This is the first time we are hearing from the company since its founder, Jensen Huang, stepped down as CEO last week. So let's check in with Colette Kress, Nvidia's longtime chief financial officer and now its interim CEO. Ms. Kress, welcome to "Mad Money."

Colette Kress: Thank you for having me, Jim. It's really great to see you.

Cramer: Thank you, Colette. The most important thing I heard tonight was that you increased your revenue growth forecast for next year. Previously, you said you would grow 70%. Now you're saying 75%, off of a higher base. How are you able to do that?

Kress: Thanks. Very, very important to understand how much our customers are interested in our compute infrastructure and how much they need the agentic solutions out there. So the most important thing that we have been seeing is just, again, a continuous growth in terms of the demand that's out there. But we also have been working in terms of our supply. So an increase in supply, working with all of our different suppliers, whether that be focusing in terms of what we need in terms of chips, what we need in terms of advanced packaging or memory, all of that is also coming together. We felt very confident, therefore, that we could establish that we will grow 75% year over year for fiscal year '28.

Cramer: Now, a lot of people have been saying that there was one man at this company. I've talked with you. There are another 49,000. How is the team holding up? Are there people who are saying, "You know what, this is not the Nvidia I know, I don't want to be there?" Is there a brain drain, as some people have told me?

Kress: Yeah, really great question. And remember, the company has been built on the perspective that employees see Nvidia as their life's work. And many of them have been here for decades, working with us from both a technology and a business-and-operations perspective. And now where we're standing is focusing on the business, focusing on getting all of that work done. And I had been working already with leadership. Leadership is supportive of everything we're doing and is standing up to help as we pull all employees and leaders together to move forward. But we have high confidence that our employees are definitely still working, still working with us, and enjoy really the work here at Nvidia.

Cramer: I have talked to you many times about the idea that the cheapest stock in the world is yours, and that's why you don't necessarily have to help other people buy your chips when you can just go buy your own stock. Where are you on buybacks versus lending aggressive amounts of money to, say, neoclouds? Because I think that the buybacks are a lot better for shareholders.

Kress: We have now been looking at the capability of making significant stock repurchases for our company. That is enabled by our significant growth and the cash we will have. During the quarter, we discussed increasing the amount of additional stock repurchases to more than $150 billion. That adds to a total amount at this point of $277 billion that we're going to be able to provide. We are completely committed to that. We do believe that that's something we're going to be able to complete all the way through, just to the end of 2027. So we are in line and continuing our stock repurchases for sure.

Cramer: OK. Thank you. That's important. And it's more aggressive than I thought. And I'm glad to hear that. Now, why are there many different reports about your company, and even about your accounting? I know you as the person who is in charge of the numbers. For instance, I read two different analysts who say you may be on the hook for about $530 billion in guarantees, which is worrisome because it could have a huge impact on your cash flow.  I heard a new disclosure tonight that made me feel like the on-the-hook number is not true.

Kress: Right now, our guarantees have been thoughtfully completed to date. And our guarantees are approximately about $118 billion, which includes one of the most important ones: a land, power, and shell backstop that we have with Portsmouth here in the United States, the best site for what we see, the future of multiple, multiple buildings working together to do that, about 4.5 gigawatts to do so. That is solely for Nvidia's infrastructure. It's working very well and is getting ready for all the builds it needs to do. And that is the most significant part of our guarantees. We will continue to do the best due diligence and thought regarding any additional guarantees that need to be done. That means we're going to be working with companies to make sure we understand where they are in terms of their land, power, shell builds, how they are doing in terms of getting ready for the compute, getting the capital that they need, and making sure that they have the end customer, the off-take that we'll need to complete that. So it's going to be a top priority. But we are all working together to make sure that we can support the most important ones that we think are running very well, and that's going to be a top priority for us.

Cramer: Speaking of priorities, from a lot of reporting, again, because I want to try to get all this stuff out. You were kind enough to come on and speak about anything unrehearsed. Based on much of the reporting over the last two weeks, it seems that the aggressive investments in the ecosystem, including some companies that are less than investment-grade, were a priority for your predecessor and his family members. I want to know if you were pushing back on those? And should we see less and expect less support for the ecosystem and more for the shareholders?

Kress: Our investments are an important part of the work we can do, focusing on a set of organizations that may be AI-native, maybe new types of companies starting, as well as helping those that want to build new types of models in the market. These are some of the areas that we focused on. But, yes, we're very disciplined in terms of how we think that through. There's a lot of discussion internally with a lot of the teams on what we think are the best ones that we want to do. And we're going to continue down that path to make sure we choose the right investments for us to work through going forward. But most importantly, these are companies in areas where we can see additional growth in AI. And I think those are important for us. But, again, stepping back to our business and how important our capital is going to be for procuring supply and getting ready for all of our employees as well, and all the work that we need to do from the engineering, that's going to be our top priority in terms of our use of capital to do so. So that's what I think is the most important.

Cramer: You are in a very competitive situation. For instance, AMD has a product that's a GPU that is much touted, and they think it can be moved in quicker. I know that some of the hyperscalers are very good at developing their own chips, which makes some people say, "Wait a second. Is what's really happening that Nvidia is supporting some companies that may not be, let's say, investment-grade or the kind of customer you would want — neoclouds — because it's losing business from the traditional hyperscalers and their shares are going down. Is that true?

Kress: Interesting statement, but no, it is not true. If we want to think about where we are with our hyperscalers, they are right now feverishly looking for more focus on the compute we have available. I have seen already with many of these contacting me and saying, " Great to see everything intact. Great to see that there's more supply. I need more demand." So they are all with us. And remember, there's a reason why. That is an amazing type of architecture that has been built through so much work with the different types of engineers. It is the most durable, fungible, and performant type of infrastructure out there. The idea that anything is changing among our customer types is just not true. They are all still with us. And we have a very deep breadth of different customers. And I think that's important to understand. These will be needed for all the different organizations overseas as well. They're going to want to say, "How do I have someone building a different type of data center overseas that they would want to see as well?" So I do believe it is appropriate to have different types of organizations that will be using this type of compute. But keep in mind, the stock, the amount of different types of customers, is broad. And we are going to continue to focus on that.

Cramer: This level of demand makes me ask you a particular question, which is that, if you were no longer allowed or wanted to ship into Southeast Asia for fear that it might end up in China, the flow back would not overwhelm pricing and drive it down, but instead would just help sate some of demand, but not all the demand? You do not need Southeast Asia to make or advance your numbers?

Kress: Well, what we are always working on is: Where do we feel we can provide the demand to our customers? We are always very, very cautious in terms of where we will be shipping to and making sure, yes, the data center is ready, and whether or not we also know that off-take and we know that customer piece of it. That is part of our process, and we will continue there. Let's just remember what we are right now in terms of our shipments to China. Our shipments to China are approximately about 10%. But that is our gaming business. That is our automotive business. That is our workstation business that is going there. As you also saw us announce, we would only have the licensed H200s [Nvidia's data center GPUs], and those went to China within this last quarter. And we are no longer shipping H200 at all, let alone not shipping it to China. So we are very careful and will continue to focus on that.

Cramer: I do want to ask you something that I think was a question that was handled by the board, but I didn't necessarily get an answer that I felt satisfactory. I understand, and have heard, that the chairman of the board says the board does not intend to ask Jensen Huang to return as CEO. But I have to say that perhaps the board would consider, after a thorough investigation — which I do not believe they did, frankly — that Jensen's value to our nation's technology, as expressed by our president today, could lead him to do something else for you. Perhaps a chief technologist or an ambassador for Nvidia's dominance who would not run afoul of either the SEC or anything done by Commerce or the Secretary of the Treasury.

Kress: Jensen resigned from his position with Nvidia, and the board accepted his resignation. The board has determined that they will not reinstate Jensen. And that is our statement and what the board has decided to do. We want to think about growing our business right now. We want to grow in everything we do with our employees, our customers, and our shareholders, and that is where we will focus moving forward.

Cramer: Do you think that it's possible that the two-way compute market project that Jensen started, that was going to be done with Goldman, with BlackRock, with Apollo, will continue? That's $500 billion in financing to make it happen the way we think it should.

Kress: Those financing funds are very important to us. We announced that they will continue to work with us, and their continued assistance with many of these companies that may be just shy of investment-grade and want to explore financing options; we're excited that they are part of this work. They are part of helping us create an asset class of our systems as well. No other company has that durability and fungibility outside of Nvidia. So they are important partners. We're going to continue working to help many of the different companies get the financing that they may want to do and the efficiency of that financing.

Cramer: You cleared up many questions for us tonight, and I really appreciate it. I know there are a lot of people who, I think, say a lot of things about your company that aren't true. I want to thank you, Colette Kress, who's been true north for me for many, many years, for as long as we've known each other. I want to say — I would say congratulations on the interim CEO. I'm glad you were on our show tonight, and I hope those who want to understand what kind of company this really is go back over what she said. #2825. Ex-St. John’s star RJ Luis Jr. debuts for LSU amid eligibility legal battle

Former St. John's star RJ Luis Jr. is officially back in college basketball.

Luis, who is at the center of an ongoing saga surrounding eligibility in college sports, played his first game for LSU on Wednesday night in the Tigers' 79-67 win over UL-Monroe in Baton Rouge, La., entering eight minutes into the game.

He recorded 11 points on 3-of-9 shooting and nine rebounds in 15 minutes in his debut with the program.

Tigers head coach Will Wade declined to address the situation regarding the saga, but said Luis — the 2025 Big East Player of the Year with St. John's — had not practiced with the team before Wednesday.

"I'll be happy to answer any questions about how he played," Wade said after LSU's win. "But I'm going to refer anything in terms of his eligibility and rostering to the university statement yesterday. But everybody we played tonight is eligible."

Tigers guard RJ Luis Jr., who scored eight points off the bench in his debut with the team, shoots over a Louisiana Monroe defender during LSU's 79-67 win on Nov. 18, 2026 in Baton Rouge, La. AP Photo/Ella Hall

Wade also said he was happy with Luis' performance.

"He played well for not having practiced in a while," Wade said. "He can shoot it. You saw some physicality and him being able to play above the rim. He can guard. He's a physical defender.

"He's going to continue to get better," Wade added. "I don't think there's any question about him as a basketball player."

After entering the game with 12:05 left in the first half, Luis grabbed a rebound and later drew a loud roar from the crowd when he hit a 3-pointer.

Wade said he noticed the crowd's reaction to Luis and appreciated it.

"I'm always happy when any of our players get recognized," the coach said.

Wade declined to discuss the reasoning that went into placing Luis on the roster this week and playing him, other than to note, "he's eligible and he played."

LSU also did not make Luis available for interviews after the game.

Luis' appearance marked the latest twist in a legal battle and opposition from the SEC in the 2024-25 Big East Player of the Year's return to college basketball.

Luis had declared for the NBA draft in 2025, but went undrafted and subsequently signed a two-way contract with the Jazz and was later traded to the Celtics. He never played in an NBA regular-season game.

RJ Luis Jr. looks to make a play during LSU's win over Louisiana-Monroe at the Pete Maravich Assembly Center on Nov. 28, 2026, in Baton Rouge, La. University Images via Getty Imag

He committed to LSU earlier this year, which set off the legal battle over his eligibility between the conference and the LSU men's basketball program.

Luis had been granted eligibility via an injunction by a Louisiana judge in August, but the SEC had publicly emphasized rules that prohibited member schools from including any player who had signed a professional contract on their roster shortly after the court ruling.

Additionally, the conference said it had the power to levy any penalties against schools that broke those rules.

Among the penalties included a half-season suspension for the head coach and the revocation of the school's voting privileges on SEC matters.

Attorneys for Luis argued that the conference had enacted the rule after Luis was granted the injunction and that it shouldn't be applied to him retroactively, while the conference said the rule had been on the books.

The legal case took another turn when a judge prohibited the NCAA, SEC or SEC commissioner Greg Sankey from punishing LSU for putting Luis on its roster, and SEC officials said Monday they would adhere to the court's ruling.

LSU president Wade Rousse said in a statement released Tuesday that the university would comply with the judge's ruling.

"LSU is committed to compliance with NCAA and SEC rules, but it is equally committed to obeying the orders of Louisiana's courts," the statement said.

#2822. Is Apple the safe haven investors think it is? Here's a way to trade it with less risk

For months, Apple has been the undisputed haven of the technology sector. As the industry grappled with the brutal reality of Nvidia's post-Huang future, investors blindly rotated into Apple, comforting themselves with the narrative that the Cupertino giant was uniquely immune to speculative overspending on artificial intelligence.

While peers bled capital into server farms and data centers. At almost 37x forward earnings estimates, the stock is now priced for perfection, fully valued at precisely the moment the rest of the market is beginning to see multiples contract aggressively. Investors tend to huddle in the shelter of perceived safe havens, but that perceived safety can crack quickly in an adverse news cycle, as Nvidia shareholders recently learned.

One part of the news cycle finally caught up to Apple.

We've recently witnessed a bizarre parade of catastrophic system failures: the massive Microsoft outage, the FAA grounding flights, and cascading disruptions across major banking networks. Through it all, Apple was immune. Until today, when a widespread outage struck, knocking out iCloud, Apple Pay, and core support systems. The official explanation? Yet another internal update gone wrong.

It's undeniably odd how all these major tech infrastructure failures are being chalked up to routine upgrades, all clustering around the exact same narrow timeframe. Without venturing too far into the conspiratorial, the sheer coincidence of these cascading digital blackouts suggests more systemic fragility than we may have realized. That's one thing at less than 10x forward earnings, as Nvidia is, or even at a market multiple. But Apple is twice as expensive as the S&P.

Technically, Apple is balancing on a knife's edge. Shares have been relentlessly hugging the upper end of several channel-based technical indicators, such as the Bollinger Band. Apple has been priced at a steep premium for being immune to what ails other struggling stocks, but is now demonstrating similar vulnerabilities. Investors should ask themselves: what's the upside? That Apple trades at more than 40x forward earnings? 45x? Even at that rich multiple, that would represent only 18-19% upside from here. If the market suddenly decided that Apple's premium to the market would be just 50%, instead of 100%, that would be less than 28x forward earnings, a nearly 27% haircut to the current share price.

Despite the high multiple, options prices are low versus the market. Market implied volatility is well above average (around the 93rd percentile). Apple implied volatility is actually just below the 1-year average. The price of index options is in the 98th percentile relative to Apple options.

Because the stock is nominally expensive (translation? The share price is high in dollar terms), buying outright naked puts is highly capital-intensive. This is exactly where a put spread makes sense. By buying an at-the-money or slightly out-of-the-money put and simultaneously selling a lower-strike put, traders can dramatically reduce the upfront capital cost. More importantly, this structure blunts the negative impact of theta, or time decay, ensuring you don't bleed premium while waiting for the technical breakdown to materialize. Furthermore, taking advantage of the natural put skew—where further out-of-the-money puts trade at relatively higher implied volatility—lets you finance your bearish bet efficiently by selling that inflated premium.

Apple's historic premium is built on a foundation of immunity to the chaos infecting the rest of the market. Today's outage proved the company may be more vulnerable than investors appreciate.

(Programming note: I will be live on cnbc.com at 2:30 talking about all of this. Be sure to tune in.)

#2821. Tre’Davious White to the rescue? Bills’ battered secondary may need a familiar face

There were a couple of surprises on the Buffalo Bills' first injury report of Week 11, with the team beginning practice on Wednesday for Sunday's game against the Miami Dolphins.

None of the starting offensive linemen were sidelined today. Well, that's not entirely accurate — right guard O'Cyrus Torrence, the only lineman not dealing with an injury last week, was on Wednesday's report, but for personal reasons rather than an injury.

But the rest of the surprises on today's report? They weren't of the fun variety.

None of these are particularly surprising. Maybe Kincaid. The Bills' top tight end seems to be playing some version of "Spin the Wheel" when it comes to injuries this season. Weeks 8 and 9, it was a chest injury. Last week, it was an ankle. Now he's keeping the ankle ailment and adding a thumb injury to go with it for Week 11.

Otherwise, these injuries were evident during Sunday's game, so it's no surprise that any of the players listed here are getting another day — or three — off.

Here, we have the group that decided to surprise this week. None of them were on last week's injury list, so the injuries all came during or after Sunday's game at MetLife Stadium. That turf is unforgiving, but not all of these may have happened on game day.

We did see Hooker coming out of the medical tent Sunday, but never got any confirmation from the Bills as to why. Now we know it had something to do with his knee.

We saw Bishop getting attention from trainers on the sideline. He was seen wincing as they manipulated his arm.

It's Hamlin that gives us reason to pause. It's not great that the Bills have three injured safeties. Plus Hamlin has spent significant snaps replacing Alford, who's dealing with a concussion right now, at nickel.

Sal Capaccio with WGR550 reported seeing Hamlin in a boot and using a scooter at the end of practice. That, information — along with a limited designation — would indicate Hamlin started practice healthy. An in-practice injury that puts him in an immobilizer is not a good sign that Hamlin will play on Sunday.

The big news here is Shavers. Head coach Joe Brady announced before practice that the team was moving Shavers to the active roster. Shavers started the season on PUP after tearing his ACL in playoff action against the Jacksonville Jaguars this past January.

The Bills thought they solved their defensive back problem. They cut C.J. Gardner-Johnson, signed Amani Hooker, got Dee Alford back from an injury, discovered versatility in Damar Hamlin, and found that rookie Davison Igbinosun was doing well at boundary corner.

Now they're suddenly facing a shortage once again. Hamlin and Christian Benford aren't a lock to play Sunday. Alford has to work through the league's concussion protocol. And, if they do play, Bishop and Hooker may not be full speed.

The current uninjured Buffalo secondary would look like Jordan Hancock at NCB, Sam Franklin, Jr. and Jalon Kilgore at safety; Maxwell Hairston and Igbinosun on the boundaries.

The answer may just be a veteran. Today, Brady said that Tre'Davious White was brought in to help this team win. On Monday, defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard said that he feels White is ready to step up if needed.

#2820. Charles Leclerc brands Brazil penalty for Liam Lawson contact "a bit harsh"

Ferrari Formula 1 driver Charles Leclerc has branded his five-second penalty that cost him seventh place at the Brazilian Grand Prix as "harsh", arguing that his contact with Racing Bulls driver Liam Lawson was "part of racing".

The Monegasque driver tapped the left rear of Lawson's Racing Bulls car at Turn 12 on the penultimate lap at Interlagos, before passing him five corners later. The stewards gave him a five-second penalty after the race, which dropped him behind Lawson to eighth.

In their decision, the stewards accepted the contact was minor, but said it had allowed Leclerc to get close enough to overtake. They gave him five seconds rather than 10, taking into account the wet conditions and the minor contact.

While speaking to the media ahead of this weekend's Las Vegas Grand Prix, Leclerc was asked whether it had been a fair call.

"From my point of view, I don't think it was," he said.

He also referred to his penalty in Mexico when looking at the last two race weekends together, but said that, judged on its own, the Brazil decision went too far.

"But if I only look at Brazil, I also believe that for me it's part of racing, particularly in those conditions," Leclerc said.

"So you've got to take, first of all, a risk and I knew that it could end in a slight touch, but I also knew it wouldn't end in shambles in that particular corner."

The Ferrari driver accepted that the stewards had a hard job.

"So, yeah, I thought it was a bit harsh, but it's also a very difficult decision to take. And I don't think there's one very wrong or very right decision, but I do believe that it didn't deserve the penalty," he said.

Leclerc is not alone. McLaren's Lando Norris, who won the race, called the move "just racing" during a Twitch stream after the race.

It was Leclerc's second penalty in as many races. In Mexico, he was given five seconds for leaving the track and gaining an advantage while fighting team-mate Lewis Hamilton for the lead on the opening lap, and finished fourth.

Ferrari remains second in the constructors' championship, 95 points ahead of Red Bull, while Leclerc is fifth in the drivers' standings, 12 points behind Hamilton.

The Celtics also have to shake off the distractions of travel and playing in front of a hostile crowd and play hard and play their game.

Officiating – I know that I say this every game, but the officiating can always be an x-factor. Every crew calls the game differently whether they call every little ticky tack foul or they let a lot of contact go and let the teams play. We have already seen games where the officiating made a difference in the outcome, both good and bad. The Celtics have got to adjust to the way the game is being called and not let the calls affect their focus or their play. The Celtics also have to be aware of the new points of emphasis for this season and try to avoid flopping, off‑arm push‑offs, reckless closeouts, delays before free throws, and illegal screens.

The Chicago Bears will take on the New Orleans Saints on Sunday afternoon, and we have both team's first official injury report for the week.

#2817. Fed’s Waller says central bank may need to ‘shock people’ with half-point rate hike

Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller on Wednesday called for aggressive action against inflation, saying the central bank needs to "shock people" as prices continue to rise more than he expected.

In the near term, the policymaker told CNBC in a live interview that a half percentage point increase in the Fed's benchmark rate is probably necessary at the Dec. 8-9 meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee.

He said the central bank needs to reverse the three quarter-point reductions from last year and may need to do more.

"I'm very, very concerned about inflation. It's kind of headed in the wrong direction, and it's spreading out," Waller told CNBC's Steve Liesman during a "Squawk Box" interview. "If you really want to get it down, you've got to start taking more aggressive actions."

"You might need to, like, shock people," he said.

Futures prices are fully pricing in a quarter percentage point hike at the FOMC's December meeting. They also are anticipating another move in January, followed by at least one additional increase before the end of 2027, according to the CME Group's FedWatch gauge.

Waller said the Fed wouldn't necessarily have to approve a half-point hike in December if it raised rates by a quarter point and signaled another move coming in January. However, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has been against that kind of forward guidance on grounds that it ties policymakers' hands.

"If you're not going to signal this very clearly to markets, you're going in January, my view is then you have to go 50 [basis points] in December to put it in place and get it done," he said.

Recent statements from other central bankers indicate a range of opinions, though most agree that more policy tightening is needed to bring down inflation.

In a speech Tuesday, St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem suggested as many as four hikes by the spring of 2027. Some Fed officials, including regional Presidents Beth Hammack of Cleveland and Lorie Logan of Dallas, have endorsed more gradual tightening.

However, continued inflation above the Fed's 2% target might push officials into a more aggressive stance.

The FOMC approved its first interest rate hike in more than three years in September, and then held rates steady at its October meeting. While inflation has continued to run hot since then, other Fed officials seem less eager to drop the policy hammer as heavily as Waller.

"I don't think the situation calls for dramatic action," New York Fed President John Williams said Tuesday in a conversation with Axios. "I think what we've been doing over the last past few months is ... working well. We're collecting the data, analyzing it, having the debate and making a decision."

The Fed in 2025 approved three rate cuts amid worries over the labor market and the belief that inflation would continue to moderate toward the central bank's 2% goal.

However, inflation reignited earlier this year after the strikes the U.S. and Israel launched against Iran in late February. Energy prices spiked while tariff impacts lingered, keeping most inflation readings above 3%.

"First of all, you've got to take back the three insurance cuts we put in last year," Waller said. "If the policy rate last summer in 2025 wasn't bringing inflation down, getting back to that isn't going to bring it down. So we may have to go above ... three hikes plus maybe some more to get it to start actually coming back down."

The FOMC later Wednesday will release minutes from the October meeting.

#2816. Rockets 119, Pacers 104: Alperen Şengün exits, Reed Sheppard gets hot and rotation tweaks

INDIANAPOLIS - Wednesday night was supposed to be the first chance to see the Houston Rockets as close to full strength as they'd been in the 2026-27 season.

With Marcus Smart's suspension over, Houston entered its 119-104 win over the Indiana Pacers with the top 10 players in its rotation available - third-string center Clint Capela (ankle) marked the only injury-related absence.

That lasted less than 1 ½ quarters. Starting center Alperen Şengün - who entered the day leading Houston in points, rebounds and assists per game - left the game after getting hit in both eyes by a seemingly inadvertent swipe by Indiana forward Aaron Nesmith.

Rockets coach Ime Udoka did not have a timeline for Şengün's potential return. Udoka said he thought Şengün, who donned sunglasses in the Gainbridge Fieldhouse locker room postgame, had a scratch on his left cornea and swelling on the right eye.

"A little bit," Udoka said when asked if it was frustrating not to have his full rotation for an extended period, "but it's good to see guys step in. … Next person up, I think our guys have lived by that all season. But it's nice to have your whole group at some point as well."

Houston was facing an even more shorthanded Indiana team missing star point guard Tyrese Haliburton, among others. The Rockets trailed for about the first two minutes but that didn't last for long - they led by as much as 21 en route to their fifth win in six games.

Kevin Durant led Houston - which had six double-digit scorers, generated assists on 68.2% of baskets and shot a blistering 54.3% on 3-pointers - with 21 points. It took him just nine shots, seven makes, to get there.

"I was just patient, wasn't rushing. I felt like last game, I rushed shots just to get shots up," said Durant, who shot 8-for-19 against the Miami Heat on Monday. "So just being more patient with my looks and holding my follow-through on my threes and I think I was able to get going from the 3-point line."

Indiana Pacers forward Pascal Siakam (43) shoots over Houston Rockets guard Reed Sheppard (15) during the first half of an NBA basketball game in Indianapolis, Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. (AP Photo/Doug McSchooler) (Doug McSchooler/AP Photo/Doug McSchooler)

Durant went 4-for-5 on triples, his efficiency from deep only outmatched by teammate Reed Sheppard, who scored a season-high 20 points on 7-for-10 shooting, making six of seven 3-pointers. The third-year guard entered the game shooting just 30.5% from deep, well below his career average. Some astute observers (me) predicted he was due for positive regression and he got it.

"Finally got some shots to go in," Sheppard said.

The guard said he never lost confidence amid the early slump, crediting that faith to his work in the gym along with teammates and coaches encouraging him to keep shooting.

Does a game like Wednesday's help the confidence?

Houston starting the game with a full rotation did give some insight into Udoka's rotation choices. Earlier in the season, he usually brought in Smart for Amen Thompson before inserting Sheppard for Fred VanVleet. Against Indiana, he brought Sheppard in first to spell Thompson and often played Sheppard alongside VanVleet - a look the veteran point guard said earlier in the season he wanted to see more often and one Houston got a chance to see in Smart's absence.

That won't always be the rotation pattern, with Udoka saying it was partially influenced by Indiana playing a smaller lineup.

"But we do like Reed and Fred out there together … two handlers, two shooters, a lot of spacing," he said.

Udoka said he liked what he saw from the VanVleet-Sheppard duo in the games Smart missed, noting Houston could put those two in a zone when the Rockets go with a double-big man lineup or play them with Şengün as the lone big. That experimentation is a silver lining amid Houston's absences in the early season, giving different lineups an opportunity to build chemistry that could help down the line.

"It's not frustrating," Durant said of the absences. "Can't control it. You can't get mad over stuff like that … We care more so about Alpi's health than anything. … Hopefully he gets right. Maybe we send him some goggles here soon, change up his look a little bit but for the most part I heard he was all right."

3-Point Goals: 19-35, .543 (R.Sheppard 6-7, Durant 4-5, Smith Jr. 3-6, VanVleet 3-7, Sengun 1-1, Smart 1-2, Eason 1-3, Thompson 0-1, Bogdanovic 0-3).

Blocked Shots: 4 (R.Sheppard, Smart, Smith Jr., Thompson).

Turnovers: 16 (Eason 3, Sengun 3, Thompson 3, Durant 2, Smart 2, VanVleet 2, Bogdanovic).

Steals: 7 (Eason 2, R.Sheppard, Smart, Thompson, Tshiebwe, VanVleet).

3-Point Goals: 10-34, .294 (Siakam 2-2, Jackson 2-3, Smith 2-4, Oubre Jr. 2-5, Nance Jr. 1-3, Slawson 1-4, Nesmith 0-3, Toppin 0-3, Walker 0-3, Huff 0-4).

Blocked Shots: 6 (Huff 2, Nesmith, Oubre Jr., Siakam, Zubac).

Turnovers: 11 (Jackson 3, McConnell 2, Oubre Jr. 2, Nesmith, Siakam, Walker, Zubac).

Technical Fouls: coach Rick Carlisle, 7:21 second; coach Rick Carlisle, 7:21 second; Oubre Jr., 4:09 third; Nance Jr., 1:04 third.

Wednesday's game was a surprisingly chippy affair considering the two teams don't share much history.

Indiana coach Rick Carlisle was ejected in the second quarter after receiving two technical fouls - the first for "disrespectfully addressing an official and for the use of profanity" and the second for clapping his hands emphatically and walking close to the official, per the pool report. Those were among the five technicals, four on the Pacers, handed out in a game that featured multiple hard falls and fouls that prompted jawing from all sides.

"Very strange game in a lot of ways … a lot of technicals, ejections, missed calls, giving the ball to the wrong team," Udoka said. "Officiated very weirdly."

#2815. The missing Gen-Z reaction that told JJ Redick this Lakers team was special

Long before the Lakers were the best story in the NBA, JJ Redick had an inkling that this team was different.

It clicked for him after the Lakers had a team dinner at Carbone Riviera in Las Vegas in July.

After general manager Rob Pelinka paid the bill, Redick became hyperaware of what had not happened that evening.

"I get up to leave and it struck me," he said. "Nobody had left. Nobody had been on their phone."

But they were indicative of the character of the group. The players wanted to bond. They wanted to be around one another.

Los Angeles Lakers guard Luka Doncic reacts to a charging foul during a game against the Charlotte Hornets, Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026, in Los Angeles. Getty Images

They were in Sin City, surrounded by a million distractions, but they chose to spend their time with one another.

Now a team that was expected to be a mile behind the Thunder and Spurs in the Western Conference has the best record in the league at 13-2. They've won nine games in a row. They've announced themselves as real championship contenders.

The Lakers have surpassed expectations. They're leading the league in offensive rating (123.1) and steals (10.8) and they're third in blocks (6.1).

Los Angeles Lakers head coach JJ Redick calls out directions against the Portland Trail Blazers in Los Angeles on Friday, Nov. 6, 2026. Getty Images

Luka Doncic and Austin Reaves constantly tease each other as though they were brothers. Their affinity for one another has spilled onto the court, where they're the top-scoring duo in the league, averaging a combined 63.5 points per game.

Walker Kessler has a contagious positivity. He's also a beast down low and a double-double machine, averaging 14.5 points and 10.9 rebounds per game.

And the Lakers' role players are starring in their roles.

That was never more obvious than in the Lakers' 118-114 overtime win over the Hornets on Tuesday. The Lakers were without Kessler (right lower leg soreness) and Reaves (left heel bruise). Doncic was in foul trouble. The Lakers trailed by as much as 18 points.

Los Angeles Lakers guard Luka Doncic, left, slaps hands with head coach JJ Redick during an NBA game Friday, Nov. 6, 2026, in Los Angeles. AP Photo/Mark J. Terrill

Doncic realized Quentin Grimes had a hot hand. He started waving off Redick's play calls in the fourth quarter, so he could feed his teammate. Grimes went on to finish with a career-high 47 points, becoming the only Laker to score 10 or more 3-pointers in a game other than Kobe Bryant in the Lakers' win.

Things have just come together for the Lakers.

There's a good feeling in the locker room. The guys genuinely like each other. And that's dangerous for the rest of the league.

"I think at the end of the day we have great chemistry, which is in my opinion very important," Doncic said. "But I think this group is very special."

It's interesting because the Lakers weren't supposed to jell this quickly.

Los Angeles Lakers head coach JJ Redick looks on against the Atlanta Hawks during the fourth quarter at State Farm Arena in Atlanta on Monday, Nov. 9, 2026. Getty Images

They have nine new players. Doncic has never been known as a vocal leader. This was supposed to be a transition year after LeBron James left in free agency and the Lakers overhauled their roster around the Slovenian superstar.

But something happened over the summer that changed things.

A seed was planted in Vegas. And it flourished after Doncic flew his teammates to Slovenia to host a mini camp, something he had never done before in his career.

They laughed. They sightsaw. They bonded with each other and grew a much deeper understanding of their biggest star.

Redick believes what's happening right now is a magical coalescence of opportunity meeting the right personnel.

It has resulted in a locker room with good vibes. A team that's soaring. And a coach who is deeply grateful that his gut feeling was correct.

He first saw it months ago, long before they ever stepped foot on the court.

"I don't know what this is going to look like after 82 games," Redick said. "I don't know what it's going to look like after 50. But I do know that there's something with this group. Every special group doesn't mean you win a championship.

#2813. Inside India newsletter: Foreign flows helped the market recover. Now it faces the inflation test

Hello, this is Priyanka Salve, writing to you from Singapore.

Welcome to the latest edition of "Inside India" — your one-stop destination for stories and developments from the world's fastest-growing large economy.

As global portfolio managers look to diversify into non-artificial intelligence trades, India, with its strong economic growth and improved corporate earnings, is emerging as a top pick. But the country's inflation, which has been rising for 12 straight months, could impede inflows.

Any thoughts on today's newsletter? Share them with the team.

Foreign investors are returning to Indian equities in record numbers, but the country's accelerating inflation, which last month breached the central bank's comfort level for the first time in two years, could spoil the party.

India's retail inflation rose to 6.09% ​in October, crossing the Reserve Bank of India's 6% upper limit, driven by surging food and transport costs.

Experts told CNBC that businesses have already started passing on increased costs to consumers, with signs of slowing demand visible in the rural economy and expected to hurt urban consumption by early next year.

"Rising inflation will squeeze household real incomes, while higher interest rates will weigh on investment and consumption, potentially putting pressure on corporate earnings," Alexandra Hermann Prasad, lead economist at Oxford Economics, told CNBC.

That could "temper foreign investor enthusiasm in the near term, even if India's structural growth prospects remain attractive," she added.

High-frequency indicators like car sales and credit card transactions softened in September while air passenger traffic declined for the fourth month in a row, Indian brokerage HDFC Securities said in a report on Tuesday.

As per data from the Federation of Automobile Dealers Associations, released on Nov. 6, car sales fell 14.2% year on year in October. The industry body said that its "pressing concern is inventory" with dealers, which was elevated at 45 days in September and October, as against the usual range of 30 days. The inflation print "is not good," Gaura Sengupta, chief economist at India's IDFC First Bank, told CNBC, adding that inflation pressures led by supply-side shocks are spreading, and if that persists, it will affect corporate margins and household consumption.

She expects the RBI to raise benchmark rates by 25 basis points each over the next three monetary policies, taking the terminal interest rate to 6.25% by April next year.

The tightening of monetary policy is also likely to slow the recovery of the private investment cycle, denting India's economic outlook, experts said.

So far in November, foreign investors have pumped in more than $10 billion net in Indian equities. If that sustains, it will be the highest ever foreign capital inflow in a single month.

This would be a sharp contrast to earlier this year in March when foreign investors pulled a record $12 billion from India on worries that the energy shock from the Iran war could squeeze the economy and slow growth.

India's growth story, however, has remained intact so far, with corporate earnings showing a sharp improvement over the last two quarters. That resilience, alongside a rotation from AI names, has drawn investors back to India, as they look to diversify into non-artificial intelligence trades.

The fall in oil prices and the easing of tensions between Iran and the U.S. after the midterm poll results have also worked in India's favor, though experts warn that it is still too early to call November's rebound of foreign capital "a structural reversal."

"November's return of capital inflows primarily reflects lower oil prices, changing global risk sentiment following the US midterm elections, and growing concerns about the sustainability of the AI cycle, rather than a clear structural shift towards Indian assets," Hanna Luchnikava-Schorsch, head of Asia-Pacific Economics at S&P Global Market Intelligence, told CNBC.

That makes rising inflation a big worry for sustained inflows. Higher inflation could further weaken household demand, prompt monetary tightening, and slow earnings growth, making the return on Indian assets "less attractive," Luchnikava-Schorsch said.

India relies on imports to meet 85% of its crude needs and around 50% of its supplies transited through the Strait of Hormuz before the Iran war. Energy supply disruptions due to the Iran war have led to a sharp rise in inflation across several major economies in the world, including India.

"What matters more for attracting stable, long-term capital, and for weathering short-term swings in flows, is whether India can sustain the high growth path it is on," Madhavi Bokil, executive director, credit strategy & standards at Moody's Ratings, told CNBC, adding that higher inflation is a risk to that path.

India's inflation crosses 6% in October after rising for 12 straight monthsIndia's retail inflation rose to 6.09% ​in October, crossing the Reserve Bank of India's 6% limit for the first time under the new series, owing to surging food prices. Inflation has been on the rise for 12 straight months in the South Asian country.

India raises export levies on diesel, aviation turbine fuel amid high inflationIndia reportedly raised export levies on diesel and jet fuel on Monday, while keeping the ‌duty on petrol exports unchanged. The increased levies on exports of key fuel items ​come on the back of rising inflation in India.

#2810. Vance scraps schedule to address tech outages as Trump admin insists incidents aren't linked

Vice President JD Vance on Wednesday abruptly canceled his scheduled appearance at The New York Times DealBook Summit to instead attend meetings on a recent wave of high-profile technology outages.

The cancellation was announced shortly after a senior Trump administration official insisted that the outages, which have affected a wide range of industries and have been felt across the country and around the world, are not the result of a cyberattack or any form of coordinated action.

"We have a great deal of confidence in our assessment that these incidents are the result of upgrades of the systems, systems being patched, hardware being applied" or other "disparate" events, the official said on condition of anonymity to discuss the government's intelligence assessments.

The official briefed news outlets by phone in the wake of numerous major disruptions at large corporations and federal agencies in recent days, including a nationwide aviation ground stop, a protracted Microsoft Outlook outage and a reported blackout of the National Security Agency's classified communications network.

Other incidents include software issues at JPMorgan Chase, an outage at United Airlines that caused some flight delays and product issues at Apple.

On Tuesday, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNBC that the outages are not a cyberattack and "not a coordinated effort by a nation-state."

He gave a similar assurance on Wednesday to the House Homeland Security Committee.

"We have no indication that these incidents are related, that they're coordinated," Clayton said. "We also have no indication that they're result of a state-sponsored malign actor."

But the sheer volume of incidents in the past week alone has raised alarm bells among consumers and tech experts alike, with some wondering if rapidly advancing artificial intelligence models are to blame.

The senior Trump administration official, asked on Wednesday's call to what degree AI was involved in the outages, said it is "challenging to answer that question across all of these incidents that have been reported."

Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, told CNBC on Wednesday morning he wants "better coordination" on AI safety.

"I understand why people are freaked out," Warner said. "The one way we could lose this AI race and [see] all of these companies' valuations plummet dramatically is if we have an AI tool run amok, or an AI-sponsored cyberattack that creates harm."

His comments came hours before before Anthropic is scheduled to price its initial public offering for the first major AI industry IPO.

Warner advocated for a "pre-testing regime" for new AI models that establishes guardrails and helps ensure a "culture of safety built in" to the industry."

He said the U.S. is "lucky" that it has so far avoided a major AI-generated cyberattack or a crisis with a rogue agent that goes beyond incidents like the Hugging Face breach earlier this year.

— CNBC's Samantha Subin contributed to this report.

#2807. Joe Mazzulla shifts blame to Celtics, not refs after Nuggets loss

Nobody buys a ticket to an NBA game to watch the referees take over in the second half. Nonetheless, the officiating down the stretch was a factor in the Boston Celtics' 105-101 loss to the Denver Nuggets on Wednesday night.

Boston got into foul trouble to start the third and fourth quarters, and Celtics wing Paul George even fouled out for the first time this season with 6:14 remaining in the final frame. Moreover, Denver attempted 22 free throws in the second half while Boston received just 3. One of those attempts for the Nuggets came with only 6 seconds to go in a one-possession game, as Celtics star Jayson Tatum was whistled for a technical foul during a late-game timeout.

Despite the fact that this final free throw gave the Nuggets a four-point lead with a few ticks left (essentially sealing the win for them), Celtics head coach Joe Mazzulla refused to blame the refs during his postgame press conference.

"We just can't put ourselves in that position to even give the refs an opportunity to interpret (it) a certain type of way," Mazzulla said, via NBC Sport Boston. "So, we just got to be better."

After Nuggets star Jamal Murray cashed a clutch jumper to put the Nuggets up 104-101, Tatum appeared frustrated and passed the ball down the court to a ref before entering the Celtics huddle. That must've been enough for referee Eric Dalen, who then gifted Tatum the aforementioned tech for perhaps bouncing the ball to an official with a little too much force.

This is partially speculation, though. Mazzulla said the controversial call wasn't explained to him, so a pool report might be necessary in order to clear things up for everybody.

Technicals and free throw disparity aside, the Celtics contributed to their own demise at Ball Arena. They shot under 40 percent from the field in the fourth quarter and missed multiple open shots. Tatum struggled to break Denver's harassing defense at times and George arguably had his worst performance as a member of the Green Team.

The C's have now lost back-to-back games for the first time this season and will finish 2026 without a single win against the Nuggets, who they haven't defeated since March of 2025. The 11-4 Celtics will look to bounce back from the frustrating loss on Saturday night, when they face the 1-13 Sacramento Kings on the road.

Listen to "On a Celtics-Mavs blowout, a Magic loss, and a Denver Nuggets showdown" on Spreaker.

#2806. One of the world's most contested seas is proving too much for Asia's leaders to resolve

One of the world's most contested bodies of water continues to cause problems for Asia's leaders.

A substantive Code of Conduct in the South China Sea does not seem to be feasible despite ASEAN nations expressing optimism that the negotiations could finally conclude after more than two decades, experts told CNBC.

The ASEAN summit in the Philippines failed to resolve it, despite Manila saying it intended to conclude the Code this year.

The crux of the issue is that China claims virtually all of the South China Sea as its own territory, despite international rulings saying it's not the case and historical claims from many other countries.

China's "nine-dash line" claim was ruled as invalid by the Permanent Court of Arbitration in 2016, although Beijing has refused to recognize that ruling.

Over decades, China has been building shoals into structures that strengthen its territorial assertions, and has become increasingly aggressive in policing the territory against nations such as the Philippines, that claim traditional rights over the maritime areas.

The Code of Conduct for the South China Sea aims to address areas where multiple ASEAN nations and China have disputes and competing claims.

Manila has reported that it had completed 80% of the negotiating text, with negotiations to continue under next ASEAN chair Singapore. But, experts are skeptical that a "substantive and effective" agreement can be realized, at least in the short term.

"It's an annual ritual. The ASEAN Chair commits to completing the Code of Conduct in January, but by November is reporting that — although great progress has been made — they didn't quite get there this year. Rinse, repeat," Ray Powell, executive director at gray-zone activities tracker SeaLight Foundation told CNBC.He described the 80% number as "a meaningless statistic," given that the issue at hand was complex and contentious.

ASEAN secretary general Kao Kim Hourn still sees potential for resolution. "I don't think it's a failure at all," he told CNBC's JP Ong. "There's still a lot of commitment and a lot of leadership on both sides to move ahead and get it done."

But Collin Koh, senior fellow at the Institute of Defence and Strategic Studies in Singapore's Nanyang Technological University, told CNBC that even if 80% of the text has been set, the 20% remaining contain the most persistent problems, including geographical scope, competing interests among ASEAN member states, and enforcement.

Koh said the original aim was ASEAN to negotiate with China "one-to-one," but, it has never been the case.

"It has always been 10 against one. Now you add Timor Leste. Now 11 against one. So, because of that, there is never any unified ASEAN position that they will bring to the table with with China," he pointed out.

Disputes in the South China Sea stretch at least as far back as the 1970s, with various countries such as Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and Vietnam claiming various zones and islands in the critical maritime region, which houses rich natural resources and fishing areas.

Back in 2015, Singapore has positioned itself as a "neutral broker" in ASEAN-China dialogue, with then-Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong saying that Singapore will deal "fairly and openly with all parties" in order to "preserve peace and stability in the region."

But while the city-state may be able to broker some compromises, the disagreements that have held up the code for almost a quarter of a century will persist, according to Lynn Kuok, Lee Kuan Yew Chair of Southeast Asia Studies at the Brookings Institution.

"Beijing, moreover, has little incentive to accept meaningful restraints while it continues to consolidate its position in the South China Sea," Kuok added.

Her view was echoed by Joshua Kurlantzick, senior fellow for Southeast Asia and South Asia at the Council on Foreign Relations, who said that a code of conduct is unlikely to happen soon, if ever. "China at its heart doesn't really want a code of conduct, and it continues to push more assertively into the South China Sea." He pointed out Beijing's actions against the Philippines in the region, including around the disputed Scarborough Shoal.

Chinese coast guard vessels have most recently been accused of ramming Filipino fishing vessels near the Spratly islands in September, and have used lasers and water cannons against Filipino ships in the past.

Kurlantzick also said that there are multiple countries within ASEAN that are close to China that are willing to hold up any agreement on the Code, adding that the move toward China is also happening as the U.S.' commitment to defense in the region becomes less clear.

"I do not think there is really any chance of a code of conduct happening with Singapore as ASEAN chair — or really, anyone as ASEAN chair," he said.

At the same time, a rushed or flawed Code would be worse than none at all, Powell said."In fact, the worst outcome is not a failure to agree, but rather a weak Code that would enable Beijing to undermine UNCLOS," he said. The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, which came into force in 1994, provides a comprehensive legal framework for oceans and seas globally.

"The narrative from China could then be 'see, now we have this shiny new regional agreement that overrides that problematic law invented by outsiders who don't understand East Asia and shouldn't have a say here anyway,'" Powell added.

—CNBC's Joanna Ossinger contributed to this article.
