#2804. Fernando Mendoza’s painful NFL debut could hold answers to next test vs Broncos

The best thing Fernando Mendoza has going for him Sunday in Denver might be the same thing the Broncos have going for them. Both sides got a good look at what happened to the Raiders rookie against Seattle.

Presumably, both sides hit the rewind button.

Fernando Mendoza (15) of the Las Vegas Raiders warms up before a game at Allegiant Stadium in Las Vegas, Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026. Getty Images

For Broncos defensive coordinator Vance Joseph, the attraction is obvious. The Seahawks sacked Mendoza six times in his first NFL start. Any coach with a rested pass rush and a home crowd willing to make life miserable for a visiting quarterback would be interested in how they went about it.

For Mendoza, the part worth rewinding might come a second or two before he hit the ground. What did he see when he came to the line? What changed when he got the ball? And where could he have gone with it once it did?

The Broncos present some big-time challenges in that regard.

"It's one of the top defenses in the league for a reason," Mendoza said. "So they are very good, they're very sound and I respect them a lot."

Coach Klint Kubiak is confident the rookie will process and adapt accordingly.

"His approach has been excellent since he got here," Kubiak said. "He's a competitor. It's his first NFL start. I thought he played well enough for us to win, especially in that first half, and we didn't close it out in the second half."

A week ago, those were questions he had to answer against Mike Macdonald's defense without the benefit of a single NFL start. On Sunday, there's at least a chance Joseph asks him something he's heard before.

Consider what Denver can take from the way Seattle made Mendoza account for pressure. A linebacker walking up to the line gives the quarterback something to think about. Put one in each gap alongside the center and now the quarterback and his protection have some decisions to make.

Michael Mayer of the Las Vegas Raiders avoids a tackle from Josh Jobe of the Seattle Seahawks in Las Vegas, Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026. Getty Images

The beauty of it for Denver is that neither linebacker has to come. If Mendoza hurries a throw over the middle to beat a blitz and finds a linebacker dropping into the very window he picked out, Joseph will have gotten what he wanted without sending anybody extra.

So where's the opportunity for Mendoza? Start with what happens if that linebacker comes.

Somebody just vacated a valuable piece of real estate. A receiver breaking inside behind him can give Mendoza a throw he can make with his feet set, before the rush has much say in the matter. Six or 7 yards on first down would do wonders for an offense that spent too much of Sunday trying to figure out third-and-long.

There's a bigger throw available, too, if Denver decides to crowd the line and leave a cornerback outside with no safety behind him. That's a chance to give Tre Tucker a ball down the sideline. The trick is confirming the safety really did come down. Seattle gave Mendoza firsthand experience with how much a picture can change between the time a quarterback calls for the ball and the time it reaches his hands.

Getting Tucker involved would go a long way, especially if Brock Bowers' ankle injury keeps him on the sideline. Tucker's ability to stretch the field, and Mendoza's willingness to take some chances on those long throws, could help open things up for the run game and the short and intermediate passing game.

Tyler Linderbaum, left, Fernando Mendoza, center, and Jalen Nailor celebrate a touchdown in Las Vegas on Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026. Getty Images

"There are a lot of variables and what our coach always emphasizes making sure we're taking the positive gain," Mendoza said. "However, those deep shots and those explosives are what can help us win the game. And so, I mean, it's really play-by-play, and I look forward to taking a look at the shots we have this weekend."

Lost in those six sacks is a reason to believe Mendoza can make some of those throws. He completed 11 of 13 passes in the first half against Seattle and got the ball to eight receivers. He already knows what it feels like to take what an NFL defense gives him and move on to the next play.

Kubiak can help him get back to that. Give Mendoza an early throw on a moving pocket. Change where Denver's edge rushers expect to find him. And if the Broncos are getting upfield in a hurry, a well-timed screen gives those rushers an invitation to keep right on going.

Some of which requires a seamless process well ahead of the snap.

"I was very pleased with him getting out of the huddle, him making the correct checks, the correct calls," Kubiak said. "That's what he has shown in practice, his ability to do that and to be able to run the show that way. There's room for growth, but in his first start, I thought that he operated the game like he does in practice."

Of course, there's a limit to what anybody can draw up if the Raiders run for 65 yards on 24 carries again. Joseph had a bye week to study the Raiders. He hardly needed all of it to see the advantage in making Mendoza throw on downs when everyone in the stadium knows he has to.

Denver figures to make the rookie prove he can solve some of the problems Seattle put on tape. Fair enough.

But if the Broncos want to borrow from the Seahawks, Mendoza gets something out of the deal, too. Somewhere in all that film of what went wrong is a throw he'd love to have back.

"The most important thing is how he's playing the game. We'll coach up everything," Kubiak said. "But like I said, and like I told Fernando, I was pleased because of the preparation that he put in. The things that he did in practice showed up in the game, and he's going to have a lot of things to learn and grow from."

#2801. Top Wall Street analysts prefer these 3 dividend stocks for stable income

Global stock markets remain volatile amid persistent geopolitical tensions and concerns about the sustainability of AI trade. Given this backdrop, investors seeking steady income can add dividend-paying stocks to their portfolios.

Tracking recommendations from top Wall Street analysts can help investors pick attractive stocks, as these experts assess a company's ability to pay dividends consistently.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Integrated oil and gas giant Chevron (CVX) is a dividend king. The company has increased its dividend for 39 consecutive years. At a quarterly dividend of $1.78 per share (annualized dividend of $7.12 per share), CVX offers a yield of 3.14%. Chevron will announce its third-quarter results on October 30.

In an earnings preview note on U.S. oil majors, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on Chevron with a price target of $241. The analyst is focused on the company's international growth prospects across Latin America, the Middle East, West Africa, and the Eastern Mediterranean.

Specifically, Mehta highlighted management's commentary on solid execution in Venezuela, with gross production expected to more than double to nearly 600 kbd (kilo barrels per day) by 2031 via three joint ventures. He also noted a recent oil and gas condensate discovery in offshore Angola and is awaiting commercial updates on the West Qurna 2 and Nasiriyah projects in Iraq.

Furthermore, Mehta expects CVX to report improved productivity and capital efficiency across domestic shale assets. He expects the improvement mainly in the Permian Basin, where Chevron projects advanced chemical treatments to drive about a 10% recovery uplift in new wells and bring down capital spend per barrel by about 25% year-over-year. Overall, Mehta expects Chevron to report Q3 2026 EPS of $4.95, above the consensus of $4.89.

"While unfavorable timing effects and volatile commodity prices may present quarterly earnings headwinds, we highlight healthy U.S. refining margins and strong asset utilization as partial offsets," said Mehta.

Mehta ranks No. 381 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 63% of the time, delivering an average return of 12%. See Chevron KPIs on TipRanks.

Kinetik Holdings (KNTK) is a fully integrated, pure-play, midstream company operating in the Delaware Basin. Earlier this month, the company declared a dividend of $0.81 per share, payable on October 30, 2026. With an annualized dividend of $3.24 per share, KNTK offers a yield of 5.82%. Kinetik will announce its Q3 earnings on November 4, with a conference call scheduled the next day.

Ahead of Q3 2026 earnings, Goldman Sachs analyst John Mackay reiterated a buy rating on Kinetik stock and slightly raised his price target to $58 from $57. He expects the company to report Q3 2026 EBITDA of $279 million, higher than the Street's expectation of $270 million but lower than the second quarter's EBITDA of $281 million.

The 5-star analyst expects Kinetik's Q3 performance to gain from higher gas volumes after notable curtailments in the second quarter. Mackay also expects the quarter to benefit from higher production and steady commodity margins, even though some lower-margin contracts and weaker Waha spread marketing gains could weigh on results.

Overall, Mackay increased his Q3 2026 estimates to reflect higher volumes, driven by rapid Permian egress pipeline commissioning, stronger throughput at Kings Landing I, and higher M2M commodity prices, offset by increased costs.

"As natural gas takeaway constraints ease across the Permian, investor focus centers on KNTK's YE26 volume trajectory and durability of its multi-year growth," said Mackay.

#2800. Retail investor enthusiasm for Anthropic IPO to rival SpaceX debut

Retail investor Dan Shetty is so eager to get in on the Anthropic initial public offering that he "drained" his Roth IRA and moved roughly $12,000 from Fidelity to Robinhood for a chance to participate.

"I don't want to tell my grandkids that I didn't invest in Anthropic and I didn't invest in OpenAI during the AI bubble," he said.

Shetty's enthusiasm is shared by many, with excitement among small investors for the blockbuster IPO expected to be off the charts. Vanda Research estimates that Anthropic could see approximately $250 million of retail net buying when it starts trading Thursday, double the size of SpaceX's IPO.

"That would be far and away the largest amount of net retail buying of any stock that we've seen in our data on the first day of its listing," Jai Malhi, senior strategist at Vanda, said in an interview with CNBC.

The artificial intelligence laboratory — which will trade on the Nasdaq under ticker symbol ANT — is selling 825 million shares at an expected price range of $70 to $78 per share in the IPO, though sources told CNBC the stock is likely to price above that range. Individual investors are expected to be allocated as much as 20% in that initial offering. And if Vanda's figures prove correct, the buying enthusiasm will be big as regular trading begins.

Founded less than six years ago, Anthropic aims to raise as much as $64.4 billion, giving it a valuation of $1.405 trillion. If demand is especially strong, Anthropic could even raise more than the record $85.7 billion that SpaceX sold in its record IPO in June.

The tech trade has been in turmoil since Jensen Huang's departure last week as Nvidia CEO raised questions about the future of AI financing. Before then, a potential slowdown in data center development resulting from Democratic victories in the 2026 midterm elections, and signs of moderation in the capital expenditures boom, had already spooked investors.

These all stand in marked contrast to the market backdrop in place at the time of the SpaceX IPO. In June, both positioning and sentiment were high, Malhi said. The Anthropic IPO could see a different dynamic, however. Demand could be strong across the entire investor spectrum given that sentiment is depressed, meaning that the bar to beat expectations is "much easier to overcome," he explained.

"What we're seeing across both retail and institutional positioning is that there is plenty of dry powder to take part in this IPO," the strategist said.

For the 27-year-old New Yorker Shetty, who himself works at agentic data platform Data Workers, this is his first time vying to take part in an IPO. He said Anthropic's emphasis on "safety first" drew his interest.

"I've been telling all of my friends, 'If you have like $5, you should invest it in this stock because this is the pure-play AI leader,'" Shetty said. "I think of my father who invested in Microsoft during the dotcom bubble, and he divested from that stock, and it was such a silly thing to do."

Joe Pak, a former macro portfolio manager who is now an independent researcher outside London, is opting against participating in the Anthropic IPO for two reasons: the likelihood of limited allocation and current macroeconomic conditions.

He believes the odds are probably stacked against retail investors when it comes to the allocation of shares.

"It's very difficult as a retail investor to actually get an allocation in these blockbuster IPOs," the 36-year-old said. "You get maybe one share, and the base case is you don't get any at all. So, it's a bit of a catch-22. If you do get a lot of shares, it probably means that the institutional bid was weaker, and in that case, you don't actually want the shares at that level."

In terms of the economy, conditions "need to be favorable" to hold a position in a stock like Anthropic, he said. But with the Federal Reserve having raised interest rates in September and widely expected to do so again next month, the backdrop could be darkening.

"The risk that you have is the financial conditions deteriorating" before the company starts to grow into anticipated profit and revenue, which would justify purchase of the stock, Pak said.

While Pak is steering clear of the IPO, he did say that at a certain level, it would make sense to get into Anthropic.

Other retail investors such as Bryan Nearnberg share Pak's view.

"I'm planning to eventually buy Anthropic, just not at the IPO price, considering when the lockups expire and there's some selling pressure," said the 37-year-old Westchester County, N.Y. resident, who works in finance operations. "We are not at the end of this short-term negative headline sentiment."

IPOs are a sore spot for Nearnberg, who hasn't had much luck trading stocks on their opening day. His skepticism toward IPOs can be traced all the way back to when he was in college.

"I didn't get an allocation to the Facebook IPO, but I ended up buying it the first day of open. I got burned pretty quickly," Nearnberg told CNBC. "Same thing with Zynga. I didn't get an allocation, but [got] burned pretty quickly in terms of price."

As a result of those experiences, "I'm pretty sure we'll see a good entry price underneath the IPO for Anthropic by Memorial Day next year," Nearnberg said, citing sour sentiment toward technology and concern surrounding circular financing as short-term headwinds.

To be clear, all the retail investors CNBC spoke with are optimistic on AI as a transformative technology — even the ones sitting out the IPO. One trader said he believes in AI so much that he uses Anthropic's Claude, a conversational AI assistant, every day.

"From a price-to-sales ratio, Anthropic's like a really good deal," Faigen said. But "it's still a massive valuation for a $1.4 trillion company, and there are significantly better deals out there if you are a fundamental investor."

Faigen, who works for an agentic brokerage firm, said he's "leaning towards patience," as he believes Anthropic is going to be public "for a very long time."

"I just am not in a rush to get in on day one based off the valuation," he told CNBC.

Anthropic's valuation depends on its ability to sustain its rapid growth. In the nine months through Sept. 30, revenue reached more than $33 billion, 1,200% above the year-earlier period. Aggregate spending commitments total about $900 billion, primarily centered around computing power and infrastructure.

Breakneck growth leads plenty of retail and institutional investors to approach not just the Anthropic IPO but the entire AI trade with caution.

"A lot of it comes down to scrutiny over how much money they're spending on AI," said Bret Kenwell, U.S. investment analyst at eToro. "Investors want to see that those investments are turning into tangible returns, into tangible revenue."

— CNBC's Charlotte Morabito contributed to this report

#2799. Kellen Moore has run out of excuses in New Orleans

How many more embarrassing losses do the New Orleans Saints have to suffer before it's time to move on from Kellen Moore? Sunday's 20-17 loss to the Carolina Panthers at the Caesars Superdome should have been the final straw.

This was a game the Saints had every opportunity to win. Carolina committed an incredible 17 penalties for 152 yards, compared to just three penalties for 46 yards by New Orleans. The Panthers repeatedly shot themselves in the foot, yet the Saints couldn't take advantage of the opportunities in front of them.

Instead, New Orleans dropped to 3-6 and watched Carolina take sole possession of first place in the NFC South.

The Saints managed just 222 total yards, couldn't establish a running game even with Travis Etienne Jr. back and scored zero points in the first half. The running backs combined for just 24 yards on 17 carries, leaving Tyler Shough to shoulder far too much of the offensive responsibility.

At some point, the excuses have to stop. Injuries, personnel issues and growing pains can only explain so much. Moore is in his second season, and the same problems that plagued this team last year continue to show up every Sunday.

And now, it's starting to regress his promising young quarterback.

The Saints have struggled with preparation, offensive consistency, overall execution and closing out games during Moore's tenure. Those are the habits of a poorly coached football team, and Moore has repeatedly failed to find answers.

New Orleans needs a change. Sunday's loss was another reminder that this current regime just isn't getting the job done. The Saints cannot keep wasting opportunities in a division that remains wide open.

It's time for the Saints to stop pretending things are going to get better without making a change.

#2798. NBA Europe appears headed for 'soft launch' next fall

Commissioner Adam Silver has said he wants NBA Europe to launch in the fall of 2027 — and it appears he is going to get his wish.

Sort of. Just not in the way he or others may have originally envisioned.

There are only 11 months between now and Silver's proposed launch date, and NBA Europe has yet to have any formal agreements with teams. Negotiations with the EuroLeague — some of the teams the NBA is eyeing are members of it — have slowed. That could lead to a "soft launch" of the league next fall, reports The Athletic's Joe Vardon. A member of one of the ownership groups of a potential NBA Europe club put it this way to Vardon:

"Broadly speaking, it is implausible that a serious league could be launched (by next October)."

The idea of a "soft launch" has been floated before and is not something the NBA has pushed back on — this was always a possibility. Building something sustainable long term was always going to take time and the league understood that.

The NBA is partnering with FIBA (the international basketball organization that puts on the World Cup and helps pick teams for the Olympics) on an NBA Europe plan that calls for 12 permanent teams and four open spots teams could play their way into through domestic leagues and tournaments. Those dozen permanent teams would be made up of some existing European powerhouses — FC Barcelona, Real Madrid, Bayern Munich, and Panathinaikos of Greece have been mentioned, among others — plus teams in major European markets such as Rome, Paris, Lyon and others (some of those teams could be tied to existing soccer powers, but not all).

What would make things smoother is an agreement or merger with the EuroLeague — the continent's existing preeminent basketball competition — but a couple of months ago EuroLeague shareholders rejected the NBA's initial proposal. The challenge is that EuroLeague has 13 permanent members and only some of them would be jumping to NBA Europe, which is a bit messy. That said, the sides are still talking, and it's possible they reach some kind of arrangement.

What would a "soft launch" look like? From The Athletic:

So, a soft launch could, in theory, include a qualifying tournament in the fall of 2027. Another possibility for NBA Europe's 2027 version is if, as expected, the NBA formalizes agreements with at least some existing European teams to join as NBA Europe licensed franchises over the next few months. Those teams could play each other in some precursory competition that ultimately becomes NBA Europe.

NBA owners are fully backing Silver and the NBA Europe plan because it's essentially free money for them. Silver and the NBA have met with potential teams and investors and expect franchise fees in the $500 million to $1 billion range for each of the 12 permanent members.

What the NBA wants is to modernize – and better monetize — the basketball infrastructure in Europe. As part of its plan, the league is looking at a multibillion-dollar infrastructure fund to pay for arena construction, including for existing teams (which may already have arenas), bringing more modern NBA-style arenas to those cities.

#2797. Michigan alumni Yaxel Lendeborg, Morez Johnson Jr. exchange jerseys after Mavericks-Warriors clash

Michigan alumni Yaxel Lendeborg, Morez Johnson Jr. exchange jerseys after Mavericks-Warriors clash appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Yaxel Lendeborg and Morez Johnson Jr. may be on different NBA teams now, but the former Michigan teammates made sure to share a moment after the Dallas Mavericks took down the Golden State Warriors on Wednesday night.

After Dallas' 116-94 win at American Airlines Center, the two rookies met on the court and swapped jerseys, with the NBA capturing the moment on video.

The exchange carried plenty of meaning for both players. Lendeborg and Johnson Jr. were key pieces of Michigan's run to the 2026 national championship, which the Wolverines clinched with a win over UConn for their first title in 37 years. Johnson Jr. had 12 points and 10 rebounds in the title game.

Just a couple of months later, both heard their names called in the first round of the 2026 NBA Draft. The Mavericks selected Johnson Jr. with the No. 9 overall pick, while the Warriors took Lendeborg at No. 11. Their Michigan teammate Aday Mara went one pick later to the Oklahoma City Thunder.

Johnson Jr. also reunited with a familiar face in Dallas, as former Michigan head coach Dusty May left Ann Arbor to take over the Mavericks.

On Wednesday, though, it was Johnson Jr.'s team that came out on top. Cooper Flagg led the way for Dallas with 33 points, nine assists and four steals on 11-of-15 shooting, while P.J. Washington added 21 points on five 3-pointers. Johnson Jr. finished with three points, a rebound and an assist while picking up four fouls.

Lendeborg was one of the few bright spots for Golden State, finishing with 13 points, five rebounds, four assists and two steals.

The win snapped a three-game losing streak for Dallas and improved its record to 8-7. The Warriors fell to 8-7 as well.

Whether they're teammates or opponents, Lendeborg and Johnson Jr. clearly still share a bond from their championship days in Ann Arbor.

#2796. Robinhood shares fall as crypto slump weighs on profits, offsetting gains in new businesses

Robinhood shares were down around 8% in pre-market trading on Wednesday as investors digested weaker-than-expected third-quarter earnings despite growth in options trading and prediction markets.

Here's how the brokerage performed in its quarter ended Sept. 30, compared with Wall Street estimates, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

Robinhood's net income fell to $468 million, or 51 cents per share, from $556 million, or 61 cents per share, a year ago. Revenue represented a 12% increase from $1.27 billion in the same quarter last year.

Despite that gain, transaction-based revenue of $867 million came in below Wall Street estimates from StreetAccount of $879 million, putting focus on whether Robinhood can sustain momentum across its trading businesses and reduce its reliance on volatile market activity.

Robinhood has been diversifying its business as it tries to expand its brokerage app into a broader financial services platform. Options trading and event contracts have become increasingly important sources of transaction revenue, while the company has continued to invest in wealth management, subscriptions and other offerings.

Transaction-based revenue grew 19% from the same period last year to $867 million, driven primarily by a more than 500% increase in event contracts revenue. Additionally, options revenue grew 31% to $399 million and equities revenue rose 41% to $121 million.

Those gains were partially offset by cryptocurrency revenue, which fell 55% to $120 million.

Chief Financial Officer Shiv Verma told CNBC event contracts on crypto movements did well in the quarter, offering investors another way to express a view on crypto despite the slump in prices and spot trading.

Net deposits on the Robinhood platform totaled $15.7 billion for the quarter, equal to a 17% annualized growth rate based on total platform assets at the end of Q2 2026. Over the past year, net deposits totaled $71 billion, representing 21% growth compared with total platform assets at the end of Q3 2025.

—With reporting from CNBC's Robert Hum and Kate Rooney

#2795. Big bets against AI debt, from CoreWeave to Oracle and the Mag 7, could soon hit the ETF market

Concerns about balance sheets and valuations in the artificial intelligence sector have hit the market hard since October, and investors who have shorted publicly traded tech companies in the AI trade have profited. Most investors don't think as much about "shorting" debt, but there will be a way through exchange-traded funds to profit from widening credit default swap spreads of top AI companies.

Both Tuttle Capital and Defiance ETFs have filed for funds that target the credit default swaps of companies closely linked to the AI trade, from CoreWeave and Oracle to the Magnificent Seven: Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms, Microsoft Corporation, Nvidia, Tesla, and Apple.

Credit default swaps are contracts in which investors pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. Wider spreads indicate investors view the bonds as riskier. CDS is a closely watched indicator of issuer health in the debt markets, especially in the AI market this year. The ETFs are designed to gain when the CDS spreads of these companies widen, either as a group in the case of a Magnificent Seven CDS fund, or individually in the case of proposed ETFs targeting Oracle, CoreWeave and Meta. The funds would lose value when the market assesses the creditworthiness of these debt issuers as improving.

Both ETF managers filed for CoreWeave and Oracle CDS funds, specifically, among broader AI and semiconductor company CDS portfolios.

If the exchange-traded fund managers get approval from the Securities and Exchange Commission, these portfolios would be the first of their kind in an ETF market that has become more aggressive in recent years about launching higher-risk strategies revolving around more complex financial instruments than just public stocks and bonds. The ETF managers plan to employ leverage in the portfolios, which both increases risk and the potential for outsized returns on any given day, similar to the way existing single-stock leverage and inverse ETFs function.

The ETF managers say these CDS funds can serve an important role in a market on edge about AI debt.

"As AI infrastructure investment accelerates and companies take on significant capital commitments to fund that growth, we see an opportunity to give investors more targeted tools to manage credit risk and hedge potential financial stress across some of the biggest names driving the AI buildout," Sylvia Jablonski, CIO of Defiance ETFs, said in a statement to CNBC.

Neocloud companies like CoreWeave are a major focus for AI skeptics, an AI bubble watch compounded by the exit of Jensen Huang from Nvidia, who is seen as a critical player in financing the AI buildout, with Nvidia called by some the "central bank of AI."

Apollo Global Management CEO Marc Rowan on Tuesday said that neocloud company AI projects could face an existential crisis if Nvidia funding dries up. "There was a strong incentive for Nvidia as a business matter to get these projects off the ground," Rowan said in an interview with CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." "If that banking function, that guarantor function, gets taken away, access to capital for a large number of neoclouds is going to disappear."

In its earnings filings and conference call on Tuesday, Nvidia shifted the tone in discussing the way it finances the AI ecosystem.

Matthew Tuttle, founder and CEO of Tuttle Capital Management, said it is less likely that these ETFs will find an audience among retail investors than smaller institutional players.

"It may be a stretch for the average retail guy," he said, but he added that having managed leveraged and inverse ETFs, it is clear that many investors "get interested" when a particular asset is seeing outsized moves, as has been the case with AI company-linked CDS in 2026. "The stuff that moves a lot is the stuff that tends to generate the most interest," he said.

Both prospectuses stress that these funds are not designed to move inversely to the reference companies' stocks and can lose money while a company's shares decline. They also note these funds don't short bonds or bet directly against a company's stock, and to buy CDS protection, they pay premiums, which are a unique cost to the fund manager whether or not credit conditions worsen.

The CDS of these companies have been on the move in a major way as part of the AI trade over the past year.

CoreWeave's 9.75% bond due in 2031 is yielding close to 16%, while spreads on its five-year credit default swaps were recently between 1,100-1,200. Spreads over 1,000 are generally considered a sign of distress.

Oracle CDS contracts have moved up over the past year from below 80 to a current range above 300.

The CDS spreads on the biggest tech companies, including Amazon and Meta as examples, rose over 100% within the past year, as their free cash flow turned negative from spending heavily on AI. Even though the market is much less concerned about their balance sheets than that of the neoclouds, major tech company CDS spreads did hit five-year highs earlier this month.

Tuttle said that these ETFs, if approved, would be the "easiest" to use for smaller institutions and family offices that want CDS exposure and "are either too small to trade with the Goldmans of the world or lack the in-house expertise to trade CDS on their own."

"It is a different way to hedge the AI trade," Tuttle said.

ETF investing experts expressed skepticism about this approach and market reception. "I don't see much demand materializing for these types of products," said Nate Geraci, president of NovaDius Wealth Management. But he added it does make sense to target these ETFs "at retail investors who are seeing scary headlines around AI capex spending. Yet another way to speculate (gamble)," he said.

Todd Sohn, chief ETF strategist at Baird Strategas, said he foresees confusion with how these funds will work. "How many non-professionals know what CDS are?" he said.

Tuttle says it won't take billions in assets to make an ETF focused on AI CDS a minor financial success. "My criteria is I want to see a runway to $20 million, which is about our breakeven. I see it here. It doesn't mean it will happen, but I think we have a decent chance."

—CNBC's Michelle Fox contributed to this report

#2792. Ian Jackson nearly killed Rick Pitino — then scored game-high 22 points for St. John’s

Ian Jackson thought he was getting benched.

Earlier in the day, St. John's coach Rick Pitino was driving back to campus from the bank when he was nearly run off the road by a BMW.

"This maniac cuts me off, almost drives me into the curb, doing 90 miles an hour," Pitino said after the No. 13 Johnnies routed Siena 119-71 at Carnesecca Arena. "About 100 yards later, he screeched to a halt, pulls over. I'm speeding after him. And Ian Jackson gets out. He almost kills me. He said, 'I'm sorry, Coach, I didn't want to be late.' He tried to kill his coach so he wouldn't be late.

"Then I got him back. I said [later], the coaches and I thought it over, because of almost killing your coach, we are suspending you for tonight's game. I've never seen a more scared look in my lifetime as a coach."

Pitino was only joking with Jackson. He started the junior, who scored a game-high 22 points and added three assists.

"I thought he was serious," Jackson said. "[I was thinking], 'Man, I messed up, I made a mistake.' I thought I had to face the consequences for it."

Asked who has the nicer car, Pitino said Jackson does.

"He's got more money than me," the Hall of Fame coach said jokingly.

Red Storm guard Ian Jackson reacts during St. John's 119-71 blowout win over Siena on Nov. 18, 2026 at Carnesecca Arena. Charles Wenzelberg/NY Post

Point guard Quinn Ellis hit his first two 3-pointers of the season.

He attempted five in the game — as many as he tried in the first four games combined. Pitino has been on him to shoot more.

"He [still] passed up quite a few, but that's him," Pitino said. "I thought he played terrific in the minutes he played."

Ellis finished with 14 points, 10 assists, five rebounds, two steals and a plus-41 rating in 22 minutes.

Freshman center Theo Edema (toe) returned after missing the past two games. He had four points, two rebounds and two blocks in 14 minutes. Pitino is concerned about his lack of stamina, as he often tires after a few minutes.

Top booster and billionaire entrepreneur Mike Repole was in attendance. … St. John's 119 points equaled the third-most in program history. The 57 first-half points were the Johnnies' most over the opening 20 minutes of a game since the first half of the 2021 season opener against Mississippi Valley State.

This week's first stock pick is Datadog, an AI-powered observability and security platform. The company will announce its results for the third quarter on Nov. 4. Datadog is seeing strong demand for its offerings, thanks to cloud migration and rapid AI adoption. TipRanks' KPIs tool for DDOG shows the growth in its customer base over the past few years amid increasing market penetration and growing adoption of its products.

Heading into Q3 FY26 earnings, Bank of America analyst Koji Ikeda reiterated a buy rating on Datadog stock and raised his price target to $335 from $305. The analyst noted that industry checks and data indicate that infrastructure software demand is strengthening, with AI increasingly driving usage and growth.

Ikeda called Datadog and Atlassian his top picks, saying that companies that can show that AI is a tailwind to growth could see their valuation rerate, even at premium multiples. He added that the total addressable market for observability is growing faster than anticipated, driven by accelerated growth of enterprise AI and the rapid ramp of consumer AI agents.

Celtics' Jayson Tatum hit with tech at the worst time of the game vs. Nuggets appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

In the fourth quarter of their Wednesday night tilt against the Denver Nuggets, the Boston Celtics were trying their hardest to not completely throw away the 17-point lead they held earlier in the game. But the Nuggets, buoyed by the support they got from the fans at Ball Arena, stormed back and even took a 104-101 lead with just seven seconds left in the fourth quarter.

The Celtics then called timeout with the intention to draw up a play to try and tie the game and force overtime. However, they didn't even get that opportunity. After Murray drilled the shot to put the Nuggets up by three, Jayson Tatum threw the ball towards an official stationed near midcourt. The referee near the baseline saw that all the way and called a technical foul on Tatum.

Murray would then make the technical free throw to give the Nuggets a two-possession lead, and that was all she wrote.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

With both teams headed to their respective benches, Tatum's frustrations clearly got the better of him. Nuggets star Nikola Jokic saw the play the entire way and pleaded for the officials to punish the Celtics star's actions. He got his wish.

Perhaps Tatum didn't take too kindly to the officials' decision to swallow their whistle on the previous possession. Celtics rookie Chris Cenac Jr. fell over on a hard screen from Jokic, which then freed up enough space for Murray to drill a tough midrange shot right in the face of Neemias Queta.

Maybe the Celtics star's frustrations came from the fact that they shot 9-of-24 from the field in the fourth and failed to execute in the clutch.

#2789. Commanders, Cowboys get help from schedule in effort to chase down the Giants

The New York Giants are leading the NFC East after 10 weeks of play, but the gap is closing. The Dallas Cowboys and Washington Commanders are hoping to take them down.

There likely will only be one team coming out of the division for the playoffs, and the Giants want to make sure they are the ones that come out on top. Here's a look at each team's remaining schedule and how difficult it will be for each team to navigate.

Current standing: 4–6, second place in NFC East

Remaining opponents: Titans, Eagles, at Seahawks, at Rams, Jaguars, Giants, at Commanders

The Cowboys have one of the easier remaining schedules in the league, but they remain in second place in the division behind the Giants. They have very winnable games coming up, with the Titans and Eagles on deck, but then things get more difficult with the Seahawks, Rams, and Jaguars before the rematch against the Giants at AT&T Stadium later in the season.

That three-game stretch before that rematch against the Giants could knock them out. Some wins against some powerful teams will likely keep them in the hunt and give them some momentum before facing the Giants in their first game of the 2027 calendar year.

Current standing: 3-5-1, third place in NFC East

Remaining opponents: Bengals, at Cardinals, at Titans, Texans, Falcons, at Vikings, at Jaguars, Cowboys

The Commanders' win against the Giants on Thursday Night Football last week kept their season alive, and their schedule is about to get easier.

After this week's Monday Night Football game against the Bengals, the schedule gets much easier for the Commanders. They will play four consecutive games against teams that don't have a better record than them, which could lead into a run leading up to the end of the season.

The final three games are a bit more challenging, as they face two likely playoff teams on the road before finishing the season against the Cowboys in a game that could decide the division if the Giants fold in the second half of the year.

Remaining opponents: Jaguars, at Colts, 49ers, at Seahawks, Browns, at Lions, at Cowboys, Eagles

The Giants have one of the toughest schedules remaining in the league, as only three teams will face a more challenging gauntlet in the second half of the season. With seven games to go, four come against teams that are likely heading to the playoffs.

If they were to lose all four of those games, they would need to sweep the Colts, Cowboys, and Eagles in order to get to eight wins. That might be enough to win the NFC East this year, but it is far from a guarantee.

The Giants should want to beat some of these top teams to give them reason to believe that they can compete in the playoffs. That all starts with this weekend's contest against the Jaguars, which is arguably the team's toughest test to date.

Kickoff between the Jags and Giants is scheduled for Sunday at 4:25 p.m. inside MetLife Stadium. Fans can watch the game on CBS or stream it on the Paramount+ app.

#2788. Fed officials expect more rate hikes, worry about AI impact on inflation, minutes show

Federal Reserve officials expressed confidence in October that further interest rate increases will be needed to stem inflation, though they decided to hold off while gathering more information, according to meeting minutes released Wednesday.

Policymakers put artificial intelligence at the core of their discussions, indicating that demand associated with the technology would be "a material source of inflation risk."

More broadly, officials said "inflation pressures in the economy were broad based" and would warrant action, with "some" policymakers advocating for a quarter percentage point hike at the meeting. A couple of participants even noted the possibility that a larger increase might be needed at the next policy meeting in December.

The meeting summary said "almost all participants judged that, under their baseline outlooks for inflation and the labor market, further action to raise the target range for the federal funds rate … would likely be appropriate, in order to ensure a timely return of inflation to the 2 percent objective."

In a CNBC interview Wednesday, Fed Governor Christopher Waller reiterated his belief that the Federal Open Market Committee should consider a half-point hike in December.

Officials at the meeting expressed a high level of concern over AI, both as a source of inflation and financial instability.

Fed staff members who briefed participants noted "that off-balance-sheet leasing commitments and circular financing arrangements among AI-related firms could amplify losses if returns on AI investment were to disappoint."

"Most participants observed that AI-related debt had grown rapidly and that much of this growth had taken place through complex and opaque financing structures," the minutes said. "A few participants remarked that AI-related exposures were becoming increasingly concentrated among a small number of firms."

Officials said they still expect inflation to fall off sharply in 2027 and beyond as the impact from the current shocks wear off.

Ultimately, the FOMC voted 10-2 to keep its benchmark overnight borrowing rate locked in a range between 3.75%-4%. Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented in favor of a quarter-point increase.

Those voting in favor of the hold "pointed to benefits in accumulating additional information, which would help in determining the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal."

Since the meeting, the inflation data has shown that the pace of price increases remains well above target.

The consumer price index in October rose 0.4% for all items and 0.3% for the core that excludes food and energy. Both readings were 0.1 percentage point higher than expected.

While indicating concern over how stubborn inflation has been, most Fed officials who have spoken publicly advocated a patient approach.

However, Waller said Wednesday that the Fed may have to "shock" markets by approving a half-point hike in December. He is the only central banker to espouse that belief publicly, though St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said he anticipates as much as a full percentage point move higher by the spring of 2027. As governor, Waller is a permanent FOMC voter; Musalem will not vote until 2028.

Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said Friday on CNBC that the central bank risks losing its credibility if it doesn't act.

At the core of policymakers' concern is whether rising prices related to the Iran war and President Donald Trump's tariffs, in many cases temporary events that wouldn't prompt a response, are instead becoming more entrenched.

Markets are fully pricing in a quarter percentage point hike at the Dec. 8-9 meeting that includes low odds of a half-point move, according to the CME Group's FedWatch gauge. Futures traders also are pricing a solid likelihood of two more increases in 2027.

#2784. CEO turned informant: How the FDA built a case against executives promising cheap medications

The federal case against an alleged illegal prescription drug operation and its two top leaders earlier this month features a notable informant: the CEO of a peer company that authorities say was committing the same import violations.

John Thomas Howard, treasurer and director of a Canadian healthcare company called CANARX, was arrested in the tunnel connecting Detroit and Canada on Nov. 8 and charged with smuggling, conspiracy and importing a misbranded drug for patient use in the United States. His brother and the president of the company, Bob Howard, is wanted on similar charges and was still being sought as of last week, according to court records.

The charges mark the first criminal case by U.S. authorities against a company that's part of a cottage industry known as alternative funding programs, or AFPs, that promise to lower or eliminate high prescription drug costs for Americans.

The cheaper medications are typically sourced from international markets, a business model that the Food and Drug Administration and Department of Homeland Security say is illegal and can put patients' health at risk.

At issue is the unregulated nature of drugs intended for foreign markets and, in some cases, the risk of counterfeit products. And while AFPs generally argue that the importation of medication is allowable under U.S. law by individuals for personal use, authorities contend the operations go too far.

CANARX, based in Windsor, Ontario, was established in 2002 and was featured in a CNBC investigation into the booming AFP industry.

Joseph Morris, general counsel for CANARX, told CNBC last year that the business was operating legally and was confident in the safety of the prescriptions it provided. Last week, Morris told CNBC that the Howard brothers "deny all the charges against them, will defend vigorously, and expect to be vindicated in court."

The FDA's case against CANARX started with a tip about a similar healthcare operation called ScriptSourcing. It is detailed in a 35-page affidavit — dated Oct. 29 and unsealed last week — written by Dustin Dobbs, special agent with the FDA's Office of Criminal Investigations.

Based in Bonita Springs, Florida, ScriptSourcing marketed its international prescription program to self-funded employer health plans. Founder and CEO Gary Becker was described on the company's website as a "health insurance and risk management consultant for more than 30 years."

ScriptSourcing had been on the FDA's radar since at least 2022 for potential drug import violations, according to the affidavit. In August 2025, Dobbs, posing as someone interested in the AFP business, emailed ScriptSourcing and asked if the company was FDA-compliant.

A ScriptSourcing employee in responses to Dobbs said the company was FDA-compliant and that it had more than 2,000 name brand specialty medications and worked with more than 3,000 self-funded health plans.

However, that same year, the agency learned of two alleged incidents in which medications from ScriptSourcing's international drug import program had harmed patients, according to Dobbs' affidavit. One patient had been hospitalized due to a small bowel obstruction after she used misbranded Mounjaro sourced by the company via a Canadian pharmacy, and another was allegedly seriously injured after receiving a counterfeit medication.

Facing scrutiny from the FDA, ScriptSourcing CEO Becker turned on the Howard brothers of CANARX.

By May 2026, Becker had become a cooperating witness for the government in its investigation into the Canadian firm, Dobbs wrote. Becker told the FDA that he had done business with CANARX on drug importation and that the company had given him a "road map" on how to operate, according to the affidavit.

ScriptSourcing provided the FDA with a spreadsheet of financial transactions with CANARX between 2021 and 2026. It showed approximately 16,549 prescription drugs have been dispensed, the affidavit said.

Then, in several recorded phone calls between June and July 2026, Becker discussed the foreign importations with the Howard brothers.

The phone calls "show that John Howard was aware of the routes for importation of drugs from Canada into the United States and has tried to mold them to fit [CANARX's] illegal drug importation program," Dobbs wrote in the affidavit. "These phone calls also show that John Howard and Bob Howard were aware that these drugs were not allowed to enter into the United States legally."

Among the shipments en route or being prepared by CANARX at the time the information was provided was a package that contained Neupro, an FDA-regulated drug for the treatment of Parkinson's disease and restless legs syndrome.

The FDA did not respond to a request for comment from CNBC on the details in the affidavit.

Gary Becker's attorney, George Karavetsos, declined to comment when reached by CNBC, but confirmed on Monday that ScriptSourcing was no longer in business.

The AFP business model was at the center of a civil lawsuit originally filed by Gilead Sciences in December 2024 that alleged several companies, including CANARX, illegally imported its HIV drug Biktarvy. CANARX has not responded to Gilead's allegations.

Gilead said in a statement to CNBC last week in response to charges against the Howard brothers that it "welcomed the government's efforts to hold accountable those whose conduct may put patients at risk."

"Pharmaceuticals manufactured for foreign markets are almost always considered unapproved and misbranded drugs under U.S. law, whether counterfeit or even if made by the same manufacturer that produced the version sold in the United States," Dobbs wrote in his affidavit.

— CNBC's Melissa Lee and Paige Tortorelli contributed to this report.

#2782. Kash Patel skips House hearing after Mar-a-Lago gala with $50,000 access

After a string of outages disrupted airlines, banks and even the National Security Agency, U.S. House members gathered Wednesday to question the nation's top security officials. But FBI Director Kash Patel was nowhere to be seen.

The night before, Patel and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin had been advertised as "honored guests" at the Big Blue Bash, a lavish charitable fundraiser at President Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago club, where attendees were offered access to a "private roundtable" and a stay at the venue for $50,000 a person.

Mullin appeared before lawmakers Wednesday morning at the committee's annual threat assessment hearing. Patel sent his deputy instead. And as the hearing got underway, a Justice Department jet that's been used by Patel before was still flying back from Florida.Flight records reviewed by CNBC show the Justice Department aircraft associated with Patel's travel left West Palm Beach, Florida, at 7:51 a.m. Wednesday and landed at Joint Base Andrews outside Washington at 10:20 a.m. — 20 minutes after the House Homeland Security Committee hearing began.

The FBI confirmed Patel, Mullin and Attorney General Todd Blanche attended the Mar-a-Lago event.

"The event is approved by Ethics, following all guidelines and regulations," FBI spokesperson Benjamin Williamson told CNBC by email, noting the gala "is an annual event honoring fallen law enforcement officers and their families."

Patel's absence drew bipartisan criticism on Capitol Hill. Committee Chairman Andrew Garbarino, R-N.Y., said lawmakers had spent months trying to secure Patel's testimony, only for the FBI director to make clear he had "no intention" of appearing.

Rep. Bennie Thompson, of Mississippi, the committee's top Democrat, said Patel's absence for a second consecutive year undermined lawmakers' ability to conduct oversight. Prior to 2024, FBI directors traditionally testified at the annual hearing.

The episode also drew attention to what was being offered at Trump's private club: a chance for donors and corporate sponsors to meet privately with some of the nation's most powerful law enforcement officials.

"Trump's Big Blue Bash is yet another fundraising event that encourages wealthy special interests, particularly those seeking lucrative government contracts, to rub elbows with officials responsible for awarding those contracts," Craig Holman, a government ethics and lobbying expert at the watchdog group Public Citizen, told CNBC.

Billed as a tribute to federal officers and their families, the second annual black-tie gala came with a price list for access.

General admission cost nearly $5,000, a VIP all-access pass $25,000 and a private roundtable with federal agency heads and a night at Trump's resort $50,000, according to the event's ticketing page. A sponsorship prospectus reviewed by CNBC advertised corporate packages reaching $1 million, including private briefings, speaking time and the chance to name and present an award to a federal agency of the sponsor's choosing.

Alongside Patel and Mullin, the advertised guest list also included White House border czar Tom Homan and leaders of Customs and Border Protection, the Secret Service, Drug Enforcement Administration and Transportation Security Administration.

It remains unclear which officials attended private meetings or which companies bought the most expensive packages. But several sponsors had substantial business with the agencies represented.

Motorola Solutions, the gala's top named sponsor, had approximately $237.1 million in fiscal 2026 net contract obligations from the Justice and Homeland Security departments, according to CNBC's analysis of federal records. That included a $139.6 million Bureau of Prisons radio contract, a $25.8 million Customs and Border Protection award and a nearly $18 million Secret Service contract option, all in September.

Motorola reported roughly $1.69 million in federal lobbying expenses this year through September, according to its first-quarter, second-quarter and third-quarter disclosures. Its lobbying included homeland security funding, communications technology and other issues.

"Motorola Solutions was proud to support last night's Big Blue Bash, honoring the families of wounded and fallen federal officers, whom we hosted as the night's guests of honor," the company said through a spokesperson. "We did not participate in private briefings."

Two other federal contractors, the Vierra Group and Teya Diversified Services, sponsored a Department of Homeland Security presentation featuring Mullin and Homan, according to the gala's published program.

Federal contracting records show Teya received three Customs and Border Protection contracts in September worth approximately $23.3 million combined for repairs at northern border ports of entry. The awards included $9.1 million for work at 12 ports, $7.9 million for nine ports and $6.4 million for 10 ports.

LEO Technologies, which markets artificial intelligence and surveillance products to law enforcement agencies, was also listed as a sponsor.

Vierra, Teya and LEO Technologies didn't immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment.

Federal ethics rules require authorization for officials to participate in charitable fundraising in their official capacities and restrict the use of government titles for personal fundraising.

Holman said companies attending such events hope to gain favor with the administration and ultimately benefit through government contracts and policies affecting their businesses.

There is no evidence the sponsorships influenced federal contracts or secured preferential treatment, and some new contract awards added to existing contracts.

The financial questions extend to Trump's own business. Organizers haven't disclosed what Mar-a-Lago was paid or how much reached the Federal Law Enforcement Officers Foundation, the nonprofit that's the event's beneficiary. The gala offered a $1 million sponsorship package — more than the charity's entire 2024 revenue of $725,476, according to its latest available IRS filing — though no purchase has been confirmed. A Republican fundraiser at Mar-a-Lago cost about $318,000 in 2023, according to a New York Times analysis of campaign finance records.

The event also may raise questions about taxpayer-funded travel. Organizers listed Mullin as a speaker, and flight records reviewed by CNBC show a Gulfstream jet registered to DHS arriving in West Palm Beach Tuesday evening, alongside the Justice Department plane associated with Patel's travel. It remains unclear who was aboard either aircraft or whether the flights were connected to the gala.

Days earlier, Mullin used a government plane to attend a Louisiana State University football game shortly after a nationwide FAA ground stop. He defended the trip Wednesday to the House Homeland Security Committee, saying government travel was required and that he personally paid for it.

#2779. Musk says Jensen Huang is irreplaceable, regrets midterm spending

Elon Musk compared Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia to kicking Michael Jordan off a team on a winning streak, while also expressing regret over how much he spent on the U.S. midterms.

"You've got a winning streak ... and then you kick Michael Jordan off your team," Musk told Andrew Ross Sorkin at The New York Times' DealBook Summit on Wednesday. He added, "Doesn't seem like a smart decision to me."

Huang resigned last week following pressure after disclosing an affair with a woman who reportedly was suspected of being a Chinese spy, alongside reports of relationships with employees. He is expected to testify before the U.S. Congress next month around national-security and export-control issues.

The SpaceX and Tesla chief executive, who previously said it would be an "honor" to hire the Nvidia co-founder, added that no one could really replace Huang.

Musk said he had heard similar views about Huang's departure from Nvidia, including from President Donald Trump.

"I think the president has voiced publicly that he thinks Jensen should have stayed as CEO, and everyone I know thinks the same ... this is, at the end of the day, the Nvidia board decision," he said, adding, "We're not on the board, right?"

Musk and Huang have known each other for years through Nvidia's work with Tesla and OpenAI. Tesla has been a major Nvidia customer, while Huang has repeatedly praised Musk's AI strategy, including Tesla's self-driving work, xAI and the Optimus robot.

Asked about the midterms, Musk said he felt "pretty foolish" about spending at least $474 million with little to show for it, though he added that "maybe it would have been much worse without that."

Musk said his goal had been to prevent the presidency, House and Senate from all being controlled by one party. "If I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money," he said.

In the same interview, he also appeared to distance himself from the MAGA movement. "I'm not MAGA," he said, adding that he wasn't sure what the term means.

On a possible SpaceX-Tesla merger, Musk said areas of overlap now exist that "didn't exist before," pointing to AI, robotics and the AI software and chip-design teams at both companies.

He said any deal would require shareholder approval and "may or may not succeed." Musk added that he could not push through a transaction that was bad for shareholders because he would "obviously get sued."

Asked whether he should receive his Tesla pay award if a merger were completed, Musk said he should not be rewarded "just for doing a merger" and should receive stock-option awards only if Tesla meets its performance targets.

Musk also said SpaceX rents computing capacity to Anthropic under short-term agreements that either side can terminate, adding that the Claude AI chatbot-maker had expressed interest in an additional 10 gigawatts.

Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 per share on Wednesday, raising $81.3 billion in what it said was the largest public offering on record, surpassing SpaceX.

Asked how he feels a year after describing his mind as "a storm," Musk said he feels "relatively at peace."

#2777. Cantor Fitzgerald's Nvidia business interests targeted in Democrats' Lutnick probe

Democrats are scrutinizing the business of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick's adult sons as they investigate why the top Trump administration official allegedly resisted cracking down on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China.

The probe unveiled Wednesday ratchets up the pressure Lutnick was already facing from inside and outside the Trump administration. It provides the latest sign that Nvidia, the scandal-scarred AI behemoth, will be embroiled in congressional Democrats' coming anti-corruption crusade, as well as a wider bipartisan effort to clamp down on AI chip sales to China.

Reps. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., and Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., the respective ranking members of the House Judiciary and Foreign Affairs Committees, are demanding reams of records from Cantor Fitzgerald, the investment firm Brandon and Kyle Lutnick took over from their father after he joined President Donald Trump's Cabinet in February 2025.

"We seek to understand whether any actions or decisions by Secretary Lutnick concerning export controls, enforcement measures, or national security policies may have been improperly influenced by Cantor Fitzgerald's holdings or business interests," the Democrats wrote in a letter sent Tuesday to Brandon Lutnick.

At the time of Howard Lutnick's confirmation, Cantor had amassed a stake in Nvidia reportedly valued around $1.2 billion, one of its largest holdings for its clients. Between September 2025 and March 2026, the firm reported a nearly 50% decline in its Nvidia holdings, a CNBC analysis of securities filings found.

In the same time period, Lutnick had reportedly been pressed to take action against Megaspeed, a Singapore-based tech firm accused of transferring Nvidia AI chips to China. The New York Times reported in October 2025 that the Commerce Department was investigating Megaspeed's ties to Beijing.

Lutnick "repeatedly stood in the way" of implementing controls on Megaspeed and other companies suspected of funneling cutting-edge chips to China, Axios reported Nov. 11.

"Secretary Lutnick's reported obstruction may have resulted in billions of dollars of restricted AI chips being diverted to China," read the Democrats' letter, which was also signed by Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove, D-Calif., the ranking member of the Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on South and Central Asia.

Lutnick's reported dithering may also have propped up Nvidia share prices for months, "preventing devastating losses for your company," the Democrats wrote.

"If these media reports are accurate, the American people deserve to know: Did the Secretary of Commerce seriously and perhaps irreversibly compromise U.S. national security interests to make money for his adult children and Cantor Fitzgerald?" they asked.

There is no known evidence that Lutnick's sons had advance or insider knowledge or information about Nvidia or the investigations surrounding it.

Cantor, in a statement to CNBC, called the House Democrats' letter "inaccurate" and said any allegations that its work has influenced government decisions are "baseless."

"Cantor holds no material proprietary position in Nvidia. Cantor's Nvidia holdings arise primarily from equity swaps executed for clients. We buy the underlying shares to hedge those trades. The decline in our holdings since early 2025 reflects the unwinding of those hedges as clients closed or reduced their swap positions, not a Cantor decision to exit a proprietary position," the company said in the statement.

"As a global investment bank, Cantor serves clients across many sectors," read the statement, which called any work with Southeast Asia-based companies "ordinary-course investment banking business."

"We are confident that a full review of the facts will demonstrate that we have operated our business ethically and in full compliance with all applicable rules and regulations," Cantor's statement said.

The new probe is among the first to be announced since the blue-wave midterm election, which will deliver Democrats control of the House and Senate come January.

Nvidia's stock has dropped significantly in recent weeks, straining the tech sector it both leads and helps finance, while raising broader concerns about the stability of an economy that has been fueled by the AI boom.

Jensen Huang admitted to an affair without specifying it was with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom U.S. officials have reportedly identified as a Chinese spy. Alice Huang and Jensen Huang are not related. Jensen Huang has reportedly engaged in at least two other affairs with Nvidia subordinates. On Tuesday, Jensen Huang wrote on X that he would return as CEO if the company's board asked him back. In its earnings call Tuesday evening, Nvidia Chair Harvey Jones said the board does not intend to reinstate Huang.

In addition to the records, Raskin, Meeks and Kamlager-Dove are demanding Cantor Fitzgerald immediately take "all necessary measures to prevent the destruction, alteration, deletion, or modification of any documents or communications related to this matter." They asked for confirmation by Nov. 30 that appropriate preservation measures have been taken.

Their action illustrates how aggressively Democrats plan to investigate all facets of the Trump administration as they home in on alleged corruption by Trump, his allies and his family.

It's not just Democrats asking questions — Republicans have also demanded answers from Huang, Lutnick and other Nvidia and Commerce officials as the Megaspeed scandal has unfurled. Huang is slated to testify before multiple GOP-led House panels on Dec. 1, while Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., has also summoned both Huang and Howard Lutnick to testify.

Earlier Tuesday, House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., sent his own letter demanding information from Under Secretary of Commerce Jeffrey Kessler regarding possible chip smuggling by Megaspeed and its affiliate Speedmatrix.

"More and more reports are coming to light of possibly extraordinary levels of chip smuggling conducted by Megaspeed and its broader corporate network, all under Jensen Huang's nose," Mast said in a statement.

Still, it's clear that Michkov is unhappy with the team's current situation. He has gone viral for shouting matches on the ice he has had with two teammates this year. His ice time has also fluctuated, though he is being used more in recent games.

This, combined with the drama with head coach Rick Tocchet last year, points to friction within the organization. Michkov is a restricted free agent next summer. More than this, he is offer sheet eligible. Michkov has a lot of say over his NHL future.

The Mammoth should jump on this if Michkov becomes available on the trade market. Utah has a very good forward group, as mentioned. But Michkov would fit in quite well with this team. He has 11 goals and 19 points in 24 games, leading the Flyers in both categories.

What the Mammoth would give up for the 20-year-old is up for debate. He certainly wouldn't come cheap. Michkov is producing at nearly a point per game and is due for a contract extension. There is a lot of value and team control there that Utah will need to factor into the trade cost.

This also doesn't mention how reluctant Philadelphia would be to do it this season. They don't need to trade Michkov at all if they don't want to, at least during the season. If a trade is best for both sides, then they can figure that out in the summer. No matter when this comes to a head, the Mammoth are certainly an ideal landing spot.

#2773. Tokenization platform Securitize gains 10% postmarket on Q3 results, move into asset-backed finance

Tokenization platform Securitize climbed about 10% postmarket after reporting third quarter growth alongside increased operating expenses, and announcing an expansion into asset-backed finance through a strategic acquisition.

Miami-based Securitize, which made its public market debut in July, operates in the relatively new corner of the crypto equity universe involved in institutional tokenization infrastructure. Tokenized assets on the platform grew 9% in the third quarter, to $4.8 billion, from the same period a year ago. Aggregate transaction volume rose 20% from a year ago, to $4.3 billion. Revenue of $11.5 million was up 28% from last year.

The growth came as bullish sentiment around tokenization gained traction throughout the third quarter, ahead of the Security and Exchange Commission formalizing the long awaited Innovation Exemption on Sept. 17, which created a temporary pathway for trading of certain tokenized stocks and strengthened the regulatory outlook.

Profitability is still meaningfully below year-ago levels, due in part to costs associated with going public over the summer, as well as the scaling up of the tokenization business at an active time for the entire sector, Securitize CEO Carlos Domingo told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

Securitize reinforced "certain areas of the company like finance, compliance, legal [and] cybersecurity," which increased corporate costs "compared to a year ago when we were privately held," Domingo said. "We're in in a very good position. The adjusted EBITDA … is improving significantly from previous quarters."

Securitize reported an adjusted EBITDA loss of $2 million, compared with positive adjusted EBITDA of $3.6 million a year ago, better than a $5.5 million loss in the second quarter. The company posted a 183% increase in operating costs and expenses.

Also on Monday, the Securitize board authorized a $50 million share buyback and announced the acquisition of River One, an institutional asset-backed financing platform developing technology to connect stablecoin capital with traditional lending markets. Terms were not disclosed.

Securitize sees an opportunity to modernize the $9 trillion market for asset backed finance by using stablecoins to finance real world assets, generate yield and tokenize investment positions and credit products, Domingo said.The acquisition also marks an expansion beyond Securitize's core niche markets at a time when tokenization's competitive landscape is growing, with traditional asset managers like BlackRock and Franklin Templeton, and established financial market infrastructure providers like DTCC and Broadridge, entering the industry.

"We have been very active in tokenized funds, treasuries [and] yield … And we've been obviously recently very active in tokenized stocks, so this adds another piece of the puzzle in the emerging tokenization space for us to capture revenue growth."

#2771. 4 Ways The Lakers Were Outplayed By The Jazz In 109-97 Defeat

The Los Angeles Lakers suffered a frustrating 109-97 loss to the Utah Jazz, failing to be efficient on offense while allowing Keyonte George to take control of the game.

Despite entering the matchup with enough firepower to compete, the Lakers never established a rhythm and fell short against a Jazz team that executed much better on both ends.

George led Utah with 30 points and 10 assists, while Ace Bailey contributed 19 points and Svi Mykhailiuk added 15 off the bench. The Jazz also received a massive rebounding performance from Mo Bamba, who finished with 16 boards.

Luka Doncic scored 29 points and added seven assists for Los Angeles, while Quentin Grimes chipped in 20 points. However, Doncic's nine turnovers and the Lakers' poor shooting prevented them from building any sustained momentum.

Here are four reasons the Lakers were outplayed by Utah.

The biggest difference was the quality of each team's shooting. The Jazz finished 37-77 from the field, shooting an impressive 48.1%, while the Lakers managed just 34-89 attempts, finishing at 38.2%.

Utah also had a significant advantage from beyond the arc. The Jazz knocked down 14 of 37 three-point attempts (37.8%), compared to just nine of 33 (27.3%) for Los Angeles.

George was the biggest problem for the Lakers, scoring 30 points on 9-17 shooting and connecting on five three-pointers. Mykhailiuk added another four triples, finishing with 15 points on 4-10 shooting from deep.

Meanwhile, Doncic struggled to find efficiency despite his 29 points. He shot 10-28 from the field and just 2-12 from three-point range. Grimes was more productive with 20 points on 8-20 shooting, but the Lakers needed considerably more efficiency from the rest of the lineup.

Los Angeles simply took too many difficult shots and failed to convert enough opportunities. Against a Utah team shooting nearly 50% from the field, that was a recipe for defeat.

George delivered the type of performance that makes life difficult for any opposing defense. The Jazz guard finished with 30 points and 10 assists, shooting 9-17 from the field and 5-10 from three-point range.

His scoring was impressive, but his playmaking was just as important. George consistently created opportunities for teammates, helping Utah finish with 29 assists compared to Los Angeles' 24.

The Lakers struggled to contain his combination of scoring and distribution. When defenders gave him room, he punished them from the perimeter. When the defense focused on stopping his scoring, he found ways to involve his teammates.

Bailey also benefited from Utah's offensive rhythm, adding 19 points and eight rebounds. Mykhailiuk provided another important scoring option with 15 points off the bench.

The Lakers had individual defensive contributions, including four steals from Matisse Thybulle, but they could not slow down Utah's overall offensive execution. George was the primary reason.

Doncic finished with 29 points, five rebounds, and seven assists, but his nine turnovers were a major problem for Los Angeles.

The Lakers committed 18 turnovers overall, compared to 23 for Utah. While that number suggests Los Angeles actually protected the ball better as a team, Doncic's individual mistakes came at a costly rate for the team's primary ball-handler.

Utah scored 29 points off turnovers, compared to 26 for the Lakers. The Jazz also recorded 11 steals, matching Los Angeles, and converted defensive pressure into opportunities to maintain control.

Doncic's offensive production was still valuable, but his inefficiency made it difficult for the Lakers to establish consistent possessions. He shot just 35.7% from the field and 16.7% from three-point range.

The Lakers need Doncic to be aggressive, but they also need him to make better decisions with the basketball. Against a team that was already shooting efficiently, turnovers were a recipe for disaster.

The Lakers actually had a 14-7 advantage in offensive rebounds, but Utah controlled the overall rebounding battle and did a much better job protecting its defensive glass.

The Jazz finished with 45 rebounds compared to Los Angeles' 42. More importantly, Utah collected 38 defensive rebounds, while the Lakers managed only 28.

Bamba was particularly effective, finishing with 16 rebounds, including 15 defensive boards. His presence helped Utah limit second-chance opportunities despite Los Angeles' advantage in offensive rebounding.

The Jazz also recorded five blocks compared to just one for the Lakers.

Both teams scored 46 points in the paint, so Utah did not necessarily dominate the Lakers inside offensively. Instead, its advantage came from protecting the rim, securing defensive rebounds, and limiting Los Angeles' ability to generate additional possessions.

The Lakers had opportunities to make the game closer through offensive rebounding, but their poor shooting and inability to consistently convert second chances hurt them in the end.
