#2770. 'Parasite' backer and other South Korean media, gaming and travel stocks rally on China trade deal

South Korean entertainment, gaming and travel stocks surged Thursday as Seoul and Beijing largely concluded a trade deal, allowing Korean companies greater access to China's vast consumer market.

South Korean entertainment industry has faced Chinese curbs for nearly a decade, and a deal stands to open up new revenue streams for Seoul's media, gaming and tourism industries.

Drama producer Studio Dragon — who created the drama Crash Landing on You — soared 29.96%, while media giant CJ ENM, which backed the Oscar-winning film "Parasite," jumped 26% early Thursday.

Travel agency Hana Tour rose 18%, while film distributor Showbox gained 9%. South Korea's gaming stocks Krafton and Shift Up advanced 2.69% and 6.57%, respectively.

Shift Up had created the action role-playing game Stellar Blade, the first South Korean game funded and published in an official partnership with PlayStation, while Krafton is the developer of battle royale game PUBG: Battlegrounds.

South Korea's Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources said Wednesday that it had concluded negotiations with China that will expand their free trade agreement covering services and investment, following eight years and eight months of talks.

Under the agreement, China has offered the most-favored-nation treatment to South Korean industries including films and games, meaning the country's businesses would receive treatment no less favorable than that granted to those from third countries.

Beijing also agreed to apply non-discriminatory principles to advance reviews of online games and films, marking the first time China has included such commitments in a trade agreement, according to the ministry.

The two countries also agreed to expand joint productions beyond films to include television dramas, animation, variety shows and documentaries.

In tourism, South Korean travel agencies operating in 23 regions across China would be allowed to directly recruit Chinese residents and foreigners for overseas travel, including trips to South Korea and other destinations.

In a Wednesday note, CGS International Securities analyst Oh Jiwoo described the move as "a meaningful step towards reopening the Chinese market," and said this also raised expectations for an easing of China's restrictions on South Korean content since 2016.

This was echoed by domestic brokerage NH Investment & Securities, which said in a note Wednesday that the agreement marked the first documented progress toward easing China's longstanding restrictions on Korean cultural content, although it did not explicitly address the resumption of K-pop concerts or the distribution of Korean dramas in mainland China.

China had imposed trade and cultural exchange curbs on South Korea after Seoul deployed the U.S.-made anti-missile system THAAD in 2016.

South Korean brokerage Hana Securities identified Studio Dragon and Hana Tour as the most direct beneficiaries of the agreement in a note on Thursday.

The brokerage estimated that Studio Dragon's operating profit could rise by as much as 50%, if Chinese streaming platforms resume airing previously acquired Korean dramas, potentially generating an additional 3 billion to 4 billion won ($2.26 million to $3 million) in revenue per title.

The Korea-China agreement has yet to be formally signed or take effect, with both countries still working to finalize technical wording, according to the ministry.

#2767. Palo Alto inks $4.5 billion deal for AI startup Applied Compute, shares pop 7% on earnings

Palo Alto Networks shares jumped more than 7% after the cybersecurity firm beat Wall Street's fiscal first-quarter estimates and inked a deal for artificial intelligence startup Applied Compute.

Here's how the company did versus LSEG estimates:

Revenue jumped 39% from $2.47 billion in the year-ago quarter.

Fears of AI-powered cyberattacks, heightened by incidents like the Hugging Face breach, are driving demand for cybersecurity vendors like Palo Alto Networks. Amid this backdrop, the company's shares have jumped 85% this year.

"As AI reshapes the threat landscape, we must continually evolve to protect our customers and enable them to adopt AI securely," CEO Nikesh Arora said in a release.

Palo Alto said annual recurring revenue for its next-generation security business jumped 66% from a year ago to $9.73 billion. Arora said the NGS ARR was one of the highest beats in the company's history.

The cybersecurity company bumped up guidance for fiscal year 2027 as businesses spend more on security in the age of AI.

Palo Alto expects adjusted earnings per share in the range of $4.26 to $4.30 and revenue in the range of $14.52 billion to $14.57 billion. The forecasts topped the earnings of $4.18 per share and $14.16 billion in revenue expected by analysts.

Net income totaled $482 million, or 57 cents per share, up from $334 million, or 47 cents per share, a year ago.

Palo Alto Networks has been steadily acquiring companies to capitalize on demand for cyber tools in the age of AI.

Arora said the company's $4.5 billion all-stock deal for Applied Compute will help businesses secure open-weight models as adoption grows. The startup helps businesses run and customize their own AI models and marks a major investment for Palo Alto beyond cybersecurity.

"If it works, I think this will dwarf the ability that we have in cybersecurity," Arora said on an earnings call. "This could be bigger than what we do."

Outages from Microsoft, banks and air traffic control have heightened concerns around cyberattacks over the last week. U.S. officials have so far ruled out any malicious activity, but experts say the rapid acceleration in patching is straining dated systems.

As businesses discover more vulnerabilities, Arora said the company expects tens of thousands of virtual patches by the end of the fiscal year. "Whatever they do today is going to take three to six months, maybe nine months, depending on how complex and how tired their environment is," Arora said.

#2766. Brian Schottenheimer has been unable to conquer this team problem

Penalties seem as old as time with the Dallas Cowboys. From 2020 to 2024, under Mike McCarthy, the Cowboys ranked first in the NFL with 570 penalties. It became a consistent talking point every Sunday with McCarthy at the helm and has continued under Brian Schottenheimer.

Penalties aren't always the defining trait that makes a bad team. The Houston Texans are second with 195 penalties since 2025, and the Denver Broncos are tied for third with 193. The combined record for both of those teams is 36-16. It's the type of penalties the Cowboys have been getting—emblematic of what the last few years under Schottenheimer have felt like.

On defense, it's the holding calls or pass interference calls on a critical third-and-long that keep them on the field and the drive moving for the opposing offense. Dallas is tied with the Green Bay Packers for the NFL lead in automatic first downs (9) given via penalty on third down. The Cowboys also lead all teams with 22 penalties resulting in an automatic first down for opponents.

The most defining penalty of the season—and maybe the culture of the entire organization—came versus the Indianapolis Colts, when DeMarvion Overshown ran out on the field as an inactive player. The Cowboys still led 20-17 at that point, but the 15-yard penalty set them back, and the offense ended up punting back to Indy, who tied the game on the next possession.

Then, late in the fourth quarter against the San Francisco 49ers, George Pickens got a taunting penalty as the offense is trying to score quickly and avoid wasting time off the clock. Instead of being at the 49ers' 19-yard line, they got moved back to the 28. It took another six plays and a precious 42 seconds off the clock.

Again, there are many reasons why the Cowboys sit at a 4-6 record. Penalties aren't the only reason they are on the outside looking in as the playoff race starts to take shape. However, penalties signal an undisciplined team, and being the league leader over the last two seasons is starting to negatively define the culture Schottenheimer is building in Dallas.

"Our second and third quarters were just nonexistent," San Jose State coach Jonas Chatterton said in a postgame radio interview. "This team's got to figure out, for some reason we just come out in the third quarter flat. … So it has to get changed."

#2762. What's ahead for AI financing after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang departs

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure hasn't produced a broad shock to the credit market, but it is putting the company's role as a financier of artificial intelligence infrastructure under scrutiny.

Huang, who stepped down Thursday amid an espionage and adultery scandal, built Nvidia into an AI powerhouse in the 33 years since he co-founded the company. Chief financial officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO as the company searches for a permanent chief executive.

Nvidia not only supplies its graphics processing units to hyperscalers and tech giants, it also provides financing to other companies to help the industry expand. That could all change.

"Although we expect the company to fulfill all of its previously announced commitments, we believe that going forward, it may be more difficult for the company to negotiate new multi-party investments among ecosystem partners at the same scale it has done up to this point," Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider said in a note Thursday.

The news of Huang's resignation comes after investors were already concerned about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure.

Tech bond yields have risen and spreads have widened on credit default swaps, most notably in lower-rated names. Credit default swaps are contracts in which investors pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. Wider spreads indicate investors view the bonds as riskier.

On Friday, the yield on Nvidia's 4.5% bond due in 2031 sat at 5.717%, nearly 5% higher week to date. Bond yields move inversely to prices.

Tech stocks slumped Friday with the Nasdaq 100 closing down 1.2% as markets continued to digest the Nvidia news. Yields on hyperscaler bonds ticked slightly higher on Friday, signaling the broader concern about AI debt lingers.

It's the smaller AI companies that could ultimately see an impact if Nvidia makes any changes to its AI financing. The company had $36 billion in off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements, or backstops, for neoclouds, according to its last quarterly financial filing in July.

Neoclouds CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN are all in Nvidia's portfolio. Their shares were down sharply Thursday.

CoreWeave, which has become the poster child for AI debt fears, saw its bond yields retreat after its quarterly earnings on Tuesday eased investor concerns. The yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 was 14.79% on Friday after climbing to 16.7% last week. The spread on its five-year CDS also dropped more than 17% week to date, although it remained above 1,000 — which is generally considered a sign of distress.

It remains unclear how Nvidia's support for those companies may change, said CreditSights analyst Andy Li.

"We don't know what the ultimate strategy for Nvidia is going to be coming out the other side," he said.

"However, I think directionally, just given the fact that Jensen was so crucial in selling the Nvidia story and being a very aggressive deal maker, it's likely that a lot of this creative deal-making and circular financing and equity and credit support is going to moderate," he added.

CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC Wednesday, before Huang's departure, that Nvidia "is not one person."

"There are thousands of people over there that interface with thousands of people at my company every day. They integrate on the technology. They integrate on the physical infrastructure. They integrate on the networking," he said in an interview with "Squawk on the Street." "They have been a great partner for us for years. They will continue to be a great partner for us."

Bob Lang, founder and chief strategist at Explosive Options, doesn't see any big changes in terms of Nvidia's relevance or its ability to finance for now. As CFO, Kress was involved in the financing deals, and the search for a permanent CEO is going to take some time, he noted.

The real issue is just how much money the company will want to lend for AI financing, rather than, say using its hundreds of billions in free cash flow for other purposes, like share buybacks, capex, or acquisitions.

"Big companies like Nvidia and Meta, they're holding all the cards," he said. "When they decide that the game is over, that's it — it's going to be curtains for some of these smaller companies."

— CNBC'S Kif Leswing and Isabel O'Brien contributed reporting.

#2761. I watched Trump, Xi and Putin gather in China. Here are my top takeaways

SHENZHEN, China — It took a trip to China for me, an American, to see U.S. President Donald Trump in person for the first time.

Trump emerged from a group of black-clad photographers and other personnel surrounding him at a welcome banquet in Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Leaders' Meeting held Nov. 17 to 19.

Seated just a few spots to his left was Russian President Vladimir Putin who picked up a glass of red wine to join a toast led by Chinese President Xi Jinping.

"At tomorrow's Leaders' Meeting, we will discuss measures to expand mutual opening up, explore pathways to innovation-driven growth, and identify opportunities to expand practical cooperation across various fields, so as to translate more initiatives into tangible results," Xi said in Mandarin, according to a CNBC translation.

Xi was speaking broadly, but Thursday's agenda includes a bilateral meeting with Trump, and their highly anticipated trilateral meeting with Putin.

But looking at the mood in the room, it seemed that their trilateral conversation had already started Wednesday night at their long banquet table. Much of what happens at APEC, including bilateral meetings and other exchanges between leaders, takes place away from the media.

But what struck me was how little sign there was of the tension surrounding Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang resignation, a controversy that has gripped markets for the past 10 days.

Ahead of Trump's entrance into the banquet hall, Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao shared a friendly moment with U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other members of the American delegation.

Last week, the U.S. officials said that Trump did not plan to raise allegations of Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy during his meeting with Xi.

It was a striking contrast to just two months ago, when I saw photographs of Huang and Tesla CEO Elon Musk sharing a table with Trump and Xi in Washington, D.C.

And when Trump visited Beijing in May, Huang took a few minutes to speak with reporters, including me, inside the Great Hall of the People. Musk was there too, accompanied by one of his sons.

This time, neither were visible in a room that was closely watched by the world. Musk was expected to join Trump's delegation in Shenzhen, but I did not see him Wednesday evening.

Their absence from the government-heavy banquet was striking. The world's most powerful leaders may be grappling with the implications of artificial intelligence, but they certainly didn't need the industry's biggest names at the table to do so.

Trump holds talks separately with Putin and Xi ahead of their historic trilateral meeting

Takaichi gets chilly reception in China on first Japan leader visit since 2019

I watched Trump, Xi and Putin gather in China. Here are my top takeaways

Why the Middle East is watching the Trump-Xi-Putin summit

Trump arrives in China for historic meeting with Xi, Putin

China's Xi calls for removing trade and investment barriers

Putin says EU is losing industry, falling behind competition

Three things to watch as Trump, Xi and Putin meet in China

Over the months I've spent following APEC's "China Year," one thing has become clear: The forum has given Beijing an opportunity to host the U.S., Japan and other member economies at a time when unresolved tensions might otherwise have made such gatherings difficult.

But even in a year defined by talks of U.S.-China "strategic stability," the APEC events have exposed the rifts and the shifting dynamics in global power. Those dynamics were on display for the opening of the APEC CEO Summit.

Several hundred attendees, from Xiaomi CEO Lei Jun to U.S. Ambassador to China David Perdue, arrived early for the opening of the APEC CEO Summit.

After waiting in silence for at least 10 minutes, the audience welcomed Xi in a distinctly modern way: by raising their smartphones to capture the moment. The applause was rather muted.

It was much the same at the more government-heavy welcome banquet that evening. So many attendees rushed to take their own photographs of Xi and other leaders entering the room that reporters' views were largely blocked.

Following Xi's morning speech, there was a lengthy intermission before Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim took the stage.

"The entire multilateral framework needs to change," he said, praising China on its "rare" recognition of smaller countries.

During the tea break that followed, attendees quickly resumed mingling. Some even brought coffee and snacks back into the room as Putin prepared to speak.

They listened as the Russian president talked about his country's economic resilience and claimed Europe was losing ground. As attendees headed to lunch, one thing stood out: Neither Trump nor any other G7 leader had taken the stage at the opening event. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke later in the afternoon.

The most visible American presence during the morning session came from business leaders appearing in a promotional video ahead of Xi's speech.

And the absence of an American voice was perhaps even more noticeable at Wednesday evening's banquet.

Trump did not follow Xi with a toast of his own. This was the same famously outspoken president, who in a winding speech in Davos, had declared that the U.S. must get Greenland.

Yet on Wednesday night in China, Trump wasn't the one holding the microphone.

#2760. Miami Heat go all out with Vice City night ahead of 'Grand Theft Auto 6' release

MIAMI — In this corner of Vice City, at least it was dry.

Outside, torrential downpours that lasted all day and had threatened flooding throughout South Florida didn't deter thousands of fans from lining up outside the Kaseya Center for a Miami Heat-Milwaukee Bucks game that was rebranded to celebrate the midnight release of "Grand Theft Auto 6." The game is set in a fictional city named Leonida, otherwise known as Vice City, that is very closely based on Miami.

The video game franchise has a massive fan base and this one has been in production for more than a decade, leading to intense enthusiasm and anticipation for the latest release. Fans, donned in ponchos and raincoats being blasted by the wind, were lined up outside the Kaseya Center more than four hours before tipoff.

More: Giannis Antetokounmpo's first game vs. Bucks takes back seat to GTA night

Inside, the vibe was euphoric and festive, and the interest in the activations was overwhelming. A custom court with electric pink and blue paint matched the pink at center court, where "Vice City" was painted in the video game's font.

Vice City-branded apparel was sold at several stores across the arena, and lines to get in to purchase items wrapped around more than half of the bowl. One fan said he had been in line for around two hours; he was still several hundred patrons away.

A store selling jerseys, the Heat Jersey Lab, was stocked only with special edition Vice City jerseys to commemorate the activation. With about 45 minutes to go until tipoff, some of the slots where jerseys had hung had been cleared out.

"This is a really unique night," Heat coach Erik Spoelstra told reporters before the game. "It's going to be a lot of fun. It's going to be a global game tonight because of the setup with GTA. I think it's awesome. I think it's fun. It's 10x to everything."

The activations were consistent throughout the night. Fast-food restaurants had been rebranded into ones made popular in the video game franchise; in sections 105, 120, 308 and 324 were "Burger Shots" and in section 325 was a "Cluckin' Bell," a fried chicken joint.

During stoppages in play, the jumbotrons above the floor played advertisements that promoted fictional businesses from the video game; late in the first quarter, one for "Status Auto Imports" was played, with the footage all being gameplay from Grand Theft Auto.

Even the Heat's public address announcer, Gale Nelson, introduced the team to fans as "your Vice City Heat." Later, throughout the night, entertainers did not mention Miami whatsoever, instead referring to the home city by the video game moniker.

"It's interesting," Bucks coach Taylor Jenkins told reporters before the game. "I'm not one to play Gand Theft Auto, never was. I was more of a sports video game guy. But anytime you can cross collaborate with sports and entertainment, I think it's a great opportunity to generate fandom for all parties involved.

"Driving to the arena, even with all the rain coming down, seeing all the people waiting outside, there's going to be a lot of electricity in here."

By the end of the night, in the postgame locker room, Heat guard Davion Mitchell asked staffers if he could keep the Vice City uniform — the shorts in particular. These are a one-off and won't be worn again. They were all black with lettering in a pink outline. The Nike logo, just below the right shoulder, was upside down.

Mitchell's request set off a series of others, from Bam Adebayo, Bobby Portis and Nick Richards. Soon enough, Heat staffers were retrieving game-worn jerseys and shorts for practically everyone.

As part of the activation, Rockstar also gifted each Heat player a custom Grand Theft Auto PlayStation 5 console with a copy of the new game.

The Heat now have two days off before they face the Oklahoma City Thunder Sunday, Nov. 22 at home. By then, the custom court will return to Miami's traditional one, and there will be no more Vice City fanfare. Despite that time off, Spoelstra isn't worried about his team spending time playing the game.

"Hey, give me a console, I'll play for the first time in my life tomorrow," Spoelstra said after the game. "It's going to be raining all day. I usually tell guys on a day off like tomorrow 'We live in South Florida for a reason. Go golfing. Go get in the sun. Go to the beach. Go out on a boat.' It's amazing this place that we live in — I want our guys to do all that.

"But we won't be able to do all that tomorrow. So if they want to go game and do that all day long on those amazing consoles, that amazing gift from GTA, go do it. Maybe one of them will invite me. Highly doubtful."

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Miami Heat go all out with Vice City night ahead of 'Grand Theft Auto 6' release

#2759. Recap: Avalanche go down swinging in Utah

To conclude their road trip, the Colorado Avalanche met with a division rival in the Utah Mammoth for their first meeting of the season in yet another start of a back-to-back. The game was physical early which led to a lot of penalties and multiple fights. Ultimately the Avalanche couldn't cash in on their opportunities and fell this round to Utah in a 4-1 final.

Brutality was the word of the night as these two division rivals got the nasty going early and often. It started with Martin Nečas who missed the puck in the neutral zone and fell awkwardly but he kept playing. Artturi Lehkonen left briefly for a puck that hit off his foot. Rookie Alex Gagne stepped up on Liam O'Brien in the neutral zone and then the Mammoth retaliated by Jack McBain hitting Gavin Brindley up high, who had to retire to the dressing room. Gabe Landeskog took a four-minute cross checking penalty on Logan Cooley but the Avalanche killed it off. There was no score on the board after 20 minutes of play but many bruises gained.

Despite the Avalanche starting the second period on the power play, it was Utah who drew first blood. Liam O'Brien sent a bit of a knuckle puck that went through Mackenzie Blackwood for his first goal of the year. Shortly after, Gabe Landeskog engaged in a fight with Jack McBain which the latter handily won.

There was a continuous parade of penalties to close out the second period led to Utah's second goal of the game. As a very short 5-on-3 expired Vincent Trocheck got a puck through Blackwood from the left circle to extend the lead to 2-0. The period wouldn't end without another fight as Alex Gagne got Liam O'Brien to drop the gloves. Neither party was very interested in throwing any punches so it ended without any fireworks.

To start the third period, the Avalanche, again, had a power play but instead of scoring gave up a shorthanded goal to Dimitri Simashev. It was the fifth time that's happened this season and now the Avalanche share the league lead in that measure. There wasn't a shutout at least when Jaden Schwartz was initially credited with a goal that went to Parker Kelly which took several hops and went past Utah goaltender Sebastian Cossa. With a glimmer of hope restored, Colorado went with the extra attacker in the final minutes of the game but Kevin Stenlund found the empty net and Utah secured their 4-1 victory.

With 11 total minor penalties called in this game, there was an opportunity for the Avalanche to turn the tide on one of their four power plays but they were the same slow, perimeter and ineffective waste of two minutes we've grown accustomed to. The icing on the cake was Shmashev going coast to coast without any opposition to score his shorthanded goal.

It's nice the Avalanche showed some fight early in the game sticking up for each other but that brand of physicality is clearly not in their nature and Utah took advantage of winning that battle.

Brindley was ruled out for the rest of the game and would be a shock if he plays tomorrow. We'll see if any other ailments come up before tomorrow's puck turn around. If there isn't then perhaps the newly acquired Mike Reilly makes his Avalanche debut as the seventh defenseman.

Another quick turn around with a game back at Ball Arena tomorrow night, November 19th, as the Avalanche host the Anaheim Ducks. Puck drop is at 7:00 p.m. MT.

New York Knicks center Karl-Anthony Towns smiles after receiving his championship ring before a game on Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026, at Madison Square Garden. Charles Wenzelberg / New York Post

●  Julius Randle, who was shipped to Minnesota for Towns, was traded in the summer to the Nets after a couple of clunky seasons with the Timberwolves. He was basically a salary dump.

Minnesota Timberwolves center Karl-Anthony Towns reacts after a foul call against New York Knicks forward Julius Randle on Monday, Jan. 1, 2024, in New York. Charles Wenzelberg/New York Post

#2756. Nvidia interim CEO Kress tells employees ‘let’s move forward’ at first all-hands meeting since Jensen Huang exit

Interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress told employees "let's move forward" on Wednesday during the company's first all-hands meeting since founder Jensen Huang resigned, a person who attended the meeting told CNBC. The person asked not to be named because the meeting was private.

Kress was joined by newly appointed board chair Harvey Jones and hyperscale and high-performance computing head Ian Buck.

Several other senior members of Nvidia's executive team spoke or joined Kress on stage, including longtime company veteran Jeff Fisher, senior vice president of software engineering Dwight Diercks, senior vice president of GPU engineering Jonah Alben, executive vice president in charge of operations Debora Shoquist and co-founder Chris Malachowsky, according to people familiar with the matter.

Kress opened with the message about moving forward and also mentioned pay raises and explained that the yearly review process, when employees typically get pay raises and are granted more stock, would be moved up from March to December. Nvidia shares are down 37% from their 52-week high.

Jones discussed the search for the next CEO, the person who attended the meeting said. The meeting lasted about an hour and was in person as well as streamed on Microsoft Teams.

The general sentiment swirling in the room, according to the person, was that employees want Huang to come back. Employees have spoken up on X in recent days to call for the return of Huang as CEO, and one senior employee reportedly sent a letter to the board warning Nvidia would lose "irreplaceable talent" if it doesn't consider reinstating Huang.

But another person familiar with the matter disagreed, saying that employees welcomed the remarks from leadership as well as the visibility into company leadership. The person asked not to be named because the matter is private.

"The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO," Jones said during the company's earnings call on Tuesday.

Some executives shared that they do not agree with Jones. "Why make such a strong definitive statement when the investigation is still playing out," an employee told CNBC. The employee asked not to be named given the sensitivity of the subject.

The meeting was held one day after Huang said he was ready to return as CEO should the board want him. Multiple employees told CNBC that Huang's letter "fired employees up."

Despite recent turmoil, Wednesday's meeting was not out of the ordinary. Nvidia typically holds all-hands the morning after quarterly earnings reports, according to a former employee, who asked not to be named because the matter is private. Kress recapped Tuesday's earnings report, calling it a "great quarter," according to the person who said employees welcomed the remarks and visibility from leadership.

In past meetings, Huang took time to answer questions submitted by employees, according to the former employee. A person familiar with the matter told CNBC that the executives also answered pre-submitted questions in Wednesday's all-hands.

Nvidia shares were down Wednesday, a day after the company reported third-quarter earnings that topped Wall Street expectations and gave no signal that the company was going to slow its growth.

Correction: This story has been revised to reflect that executives at Nvidia's all-hands meeting answered employee questions. A previous version mischaracterized how executives handled employee questions.

#2755. 10 Takeaways: Too Many Guys Had Off Nights For Avalanche

For all the good things the Avalanche did in the first game and a half without Nathan MacKinnon and Cale Makar, Wednesday night in Utah was a significant step backward.

Colorado lost 4-1 to the Mammoth at Delta Center and didn't have much of an answer for its division rival. Utah nearly shut out the Avalanche and did an excellent job keeping Colorado's most important offensive players in check.

On most nights, the team with more passengers is usually going to lose. That becomes an even bigger problem when you're already missing two of the best players in the world. Colorado had too many passengers Wednesday, and it showed. It's unacceptable.

Read NextPostgame Reaction: Avalanche Got Beat Up, Frustrated in Utah

1. It started with the top guys. I don't think any of Martin Necas, Nazem Kadri, Brock Nelson or T.J. Hughes had particularly good nights offensively. Those are the players Colorado needs to lean on with MacKinnon and Makar out of the lineup. Most of them also make up the top power-play unit, which head coach Jared Bednar didn't seem to trust in the later stages of the game. That's not a great sign.

2. The Avalanche had a full two-minute power play to begin the third period, and Bednar started with his second unit. Once the top group got on the ice, Kadri and Necas were both slow getting back defensively, allowing Dmitri Simashev to fire the puck past Mackenzie Blackwood for a shorthanded goal that essentially put the game out of reach. That's a shot Blackwood probably wants back, but it was also a brutal breakdown by the power-play unit. Bednar went right back to PP2 after the goal. You have to imagine he wasn't happy with how that played out.

3. I'd guess just about everyone in the Avalanche organization was infuriated by the hit that knocked Gavin Brindley out of the game. Jack McBain caught him late, and Brindley was completely blindsided. I'm sure the young forward will be reminded that he needs to be aware of his surroundings at all times, but that doesn't take away from the fact that he shouldn't have been expecting a hit in that moment. In many ways, this was the sequence that rattled the Avalanche and changed the temperature of the game.

4. Gabe Landeskog wasn't going to let that hit go unanswered. Kudos to the captain for challenging McBain, who has a significant advantage in both size and fighting ability. McBain got the better of that fight, no question. It was frustrating to watch Landeskog struggle to regain his footing a few times as the two went at it. The captain deserves credit for standing up for his teammate, but it was still a difficult scene to watch.

5. Corey Masisak of the Denver Post got a great quote from Landeskog after the game.

Avs Gabe Landeskog on the hit on Gavin Brindley: "I've seen guys get suspended for less."

— Corey Masisak (@cmasisak22) November 19, 2026

6. On a positive note, it was great to see Alex Gagne get so much national recognition on TNT. The broadcast crew was singing his praises for playing a sound defensive game, getting involved physically and showing a willingness to stick up for a teammate. It's encouraging to see a rookie defenseman making that kind of impression.

7. Gagne fought Liam O'Brien, who isn't an easy opponent by any means. That's a pretty significant challenge for a rookie, and it's the kind of thing his teammates have to appreciate.

8. It's hard to believe the Avalanche had 31 shots in this game. It felt like they had very little going offensively after the first period and didn't challenge Sebastian Cossa nearly enough. Even in the opening 20 minutes, Utah had an 11-4 advantage in high-danger chances. Colorado's offense never consistently generated the kind of pressure you'd expect from a team trying to get back into a game.

9. Many of you know I'm not a fan of power plays that carry over from one period to the next. But it's not every day you get a full two-minute power play to start two consecutive periods. You have to take advantage of at least one of those opportunities. Instead, the Avalanche came away empty-handed on both and gave up a shorthanded goal on the second.

The Seattle Seahawks took care of the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday, assuring themselves of a winning record entering the bye. It was a game of few offensive snaps for both teams in what was a tale of two halves, as the Seahawks controlled the second half while the Raiders weren't short on time with the ball in the first half.

As a result, the only players who played north of 50 offensive snaps for Seattle were Drew Lock, plus every starting offensive lineman except Abe Lucas.

Seattle leaned heavily on having 12 and 13 personnel sets in this one, with Nick Kallerup managing to outsnap Rashid Shaheed even after missing the end of the game with a minor ankle injury. Shaheed's return also meant Tory Horton was back to a distant WR4 status with only 10 snaps played. #2753. Takaichi gets chilly reception in China on first Japan leader visit since 2019

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi received a subdued welcome on her first trip to China as premier, signaling Beijing's limited appetite for repairing ties strained by a simmering row over Taiwan.

At gatherings such as this week's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, protocol details — including who greets a visiting leader at the airport and where they are positioned in official photographs — often convey political messages.

Takaichi was met on the tarmac Wednesday by a retired Chinese diplomat, rather than a serving official, and Japan's ambassador to China, Kenji Kanasugi.

The low-key reception contrasted sharply with the warmer welcomes given to other visiting leaders, including South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, while U.S. President Donald Trump was greeted personally by Chinese President Xi Jinping.

In the leaders' group photo, Takaichi was placed in the back row, off to the side and several places from Xi, who stood alongside Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

"Beijing sought to downgrade her official status to that of a head of government rather than a head of state," said Jeremy Chan, senior analyst at Eurasia Group.

During Thursday morning's greeting line, Takaichi spent several minutes trying to talk to the Chinese leader without an interpreter present, while most leaders exchanged handshakes and kept walking.

"It has become increasingly difficult for her to engage in formal or even informal conversations with Xi," said Kei Koga, an associate professor at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore, who sees Takaichi's intention as to still "project the image that she could still communicate with him despite the ongoing tensions."

Takaichi's subdued reception signaled Beijing's lack of enthusiasm to repair ties with Tokyo, analysts said, potentially prolonging China's curbs on critical mineral exports that have gripped Japanese industries for the past year.

"China's frosty reception of Takaichi shows quite clearly that Beijing is not yet ready to forgive her over her remarks about Taiwan," Chan said, expecting the bilateral relationship to remain strained until Takaichi leaves office.

That could leave Japan grappling with continued restrictions on rare earth supplies from China next year, said Tianchen Xu, senior economist at the Economist Intelligence Unit.

Relations deteriorated sharply after Takaichi said in November 2025 that a Taiwan Strait crisis could constitute a situation threatening Japan's survival and warrant a self-defense response.

While the substance broadly aligned with Japan's existing security policy, previous prime ministers had generally avoided stating it so explicitly in a Taiwan scenario.

China reacted angrily and demanded that Takaichi retract the remarks. She has not done so, while stating that the door to dialogue with Beijing remains open, with minimal high-level contact over the past year.

China has since tightened restrictions affecting Japan, including controls on dual-use and rare earth exports with potential military uses. It also discouraged its citizens from traveling to Japan and halted Japanese seafood imports.

Takaichi's visit marked the first trip to China by a Japanese prime minister since Shinzo Abe traveled to Chengdu in December 2019 for a trilateral summit with Chinese and South Korean leaders.

No formal Takaichi-Xi meeting has been publicly scheduled during her visit. Meanwhile, Xi is expected to join Trump and Putin for a historic trilateral gathering on Thursday, alongside a bilateral meeting with Trump.

Takaichi needs to show a "reflection of what she said about Taiwan a year ago," said Huiyao Wang, founder of the Beijing-based Center for China and Globalization, which is often seen as close to Beijing's thinking.

Wang said Tokyo should show greater flexibility, pointing to Trump's comments that the U.S. would avoid getting involved in the Taiwan issue. He argued that Japan holding firm on the issue would not help relations with Beijing.

Such reflection, he said, "would really help to clarify some of those misunderstandings between the two countries."

#2750. Week 10 Observations: I Like That!

The Vikings began the unexpected second act of their 2026 season with a resounding 30-10 road victory over the rival Green Bay Packers. Between Kirk Cousins' emotional return and the defense's historic season, it's hard to imagine a more memorable and satisfying result.

The Daily Norseman crew did their usual stellar job recapping the rewarding victory here, here, and here. Aside from the obvious candidates (e.g., Turner, Van Ginkel, Redmond, Smith, Wilson, Van Noy, Price), I was particularly encouraged by contributions from Caleb Banks, Elijah Williams, Gavin Bartholomew, Tai Felton, and Jakobe Thomas. Maybe we do have some depth, huh?

Like He Never Left. Kirk Cousins parachuted into Vikings practice on Wednesday and started on Sunday. As unheard of as that is, given the chaos that's defined the past two seasons at quarterback, seeing him run out to the huddle for the opening series felt totally normal, as if time stood still. I was eagerly soaking it all in.

Even with a few days of prep and a playbook that had changed since 2023, Cousins' familiarity with the scheme and system was evident from the get-go. While the numbers weren't overwhelming – 21 for 31, 207 yards, 2 TDs, and an interception – the eye test was passed with flying colors.

Of course, not all passes and not all yards gained on them are created equal. How and when matter. That's where Cousins immediately changed things. EPA per play improved (+0.04), and the Vikings offense converted 8-of-16 third downs. This included a 3rd-and-23 TD to Myles Price and a critical 3rd-and-12 conversion to Justin Jefferson, who also saw a season-high number of targets. Coincidence? I think not. This was a notable improvement over the 3-for-10 third-down conversion rate in the loss to the Lions and the 3-for-11 in the ugly win against the Colts. The Bills game? Let's not go there.

It's also no fluke that Sunday's game saw the Vikings' offensive time of possession jump to over 35 minutes. This was a marked improvement over the abysmal 17 minutes against the Bills and 24 minutes against the Lions, respectively, in the team's two losses. It was also much better than the 28 minutes in the ugly home win over the hapless Colts. It's almost as if the mere threat of an effective passing game suddenly makes running the ball easier. Weird.

It's just one week, and time will tell, but based on interviews and body language, this seems like a different Kirk Cousins to me. One who is not only more confident and comfortable but also grateful for the opportunity to change the narrative of his career forever – something that seemed out of reach just days earlier. All made easier by what's shaping up to be a historic defense by his side. I basically said it all last week:

Cousins realizes the feel-good, storybook ending is within reach. Reports say the Raiders left the trade decision in his hands. He knows. This is his last, best chance. A Kirk Cousins with a Super Bowl ring would not only have a legitimate Hall of Fame resume (the statistics will be there), but he'd also have a statue outside U.S. Stadium to immortalize his role in ending the long-suffering anguish of a tortured fan base.

I've Seen Enough. This Defense is Generational. After another impressive performance against a top-flight offense, it's time to discuss the 2026 Minnesota Vikings' defense in historic terms.

While national media talking heads usually write narrative checks on the Packers that they inevitably can't cash, it was worse coming into Sunday's game because the Packers had won five of their last six, including a dominant win over a fraudulent Patriots team living off last season's rep the week prior. Instead, they got another kind of check: a reality check.

The eight sacks and four turnovers didn't do justice to the torture Brian Flores inflicted on Matt LaFleur, Jordan Love, and the entire Packers offense throughout the afternoon. It was yet another piece of the puzzle that, when complete, could look record-breaking.

The comparison to the 1985 Bears is impressive enough, especially given the changes made to benefit offenses over the past 20 years.

Enjoy the rest of the ride, folks. Soak it all in, because this isn't normal. It's thrilling, but it's not guaranteed to last beyond this season. Brian Flores will get another head-coaching opportunity someday, and key players such as Blake Cashman, Andrew Van Ginkel, Isaiah Rodgers, and Kyle Van Noy will be free agents. Meanwhile, Jalen Redmond is a restricted free agent, and it's almost certainly Harrison Smith's last hurrah.

Third Time a Charm? Since 1990, the Vikings have made the playoffs 17 times, tying for 7th in that span. Not too shabby. Each year, the purple neurons in my brain lit up, distorting reality into something that justified the belief that they could not only make the Super Bowl but win it.

My intuition has proven far more reliable. It's equipped with the right defenses to filter out most delusions and purify it all. It shocks me back into reality, takes off the blinders so I can see clearly, and acknowledges the issues you know deep down will inevitably dash the dream.

They truly aligned only twice: 1998 and 2009. Not 2000. Not 2017. My gut didn't trust the defense in 2000 or the offense in 2017. In the end, both sides of the ball were an issue, but that doesn't matter now.

What matters is… things are close to aligning with this team again after 17 years. The convergence of multiple elements (i.e., the defense and Cousins' return) for a magical season appears to be in place. There are still eight games left, so that could change before the playoffs, and that very well could happen. But I've never been as close to the long-awaited third instance as I was after this impressive win in Green Bay. A win, or even a razor-thin loss, to the 8-1 49ers next week will put it within arm's reach.

If so, let's hope the third time is the charm and that the season ends with a third act, one that culminates in a Lombardi Trophy triumphantly lifted in the air.

A whole host of NBA franchises spent the past couple of years rebuilding, seemingly a third of the league trying to tank their way to top-end talent.

The Nets were one of those teams. And amid their disappointing start to the season, this week has seen them take on — and be weighed and measured against — a couple of squads who took almost identical approaches.

Brooklyn came up short over the weekend in Memphis. And discounting Monday's loss to the 76ers — a contender on a different timeline — the Nets had another chance to test themselves against a tank rival Wednesday when they hosted the Bulls, but flopped, once again, suffering a 137-107 blowout loss.

Nets guard Nolan Traore (10) is guarded by Chicago Bulls center Nic Claxton (9) and guard Norman Powell (24). IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

An uninspiring 3-10 record heading into Wednesday — along with spotty performances from the horde of young first-round talents upon which this rebuild is based — begs legitimate questions for the big picture.

"I'm not sure we're going to be any more active than we've been in the past, but that doesn't mean we're not listening. That doesn't mean we're not shaking trees and seeing what's out there," GM Sean Marks had said. "A lot will be predicated first and foremost on what this roster looks like, and we'll get a good feel for that pretty early."

Brooklyn had seven first-round picks the past two years. After having the sixth-best lottery odds in 2025, they fell to eighth and took Egor Dëmin. And after having the joint-top odds this year, they tumbled to sixth and selected Mikel Brown Jr.

The latter had logged just 200 minutes in nine games, missing four and having his playing time curbed. And the former dealt with a bone bruise this season and a disappointing start, chastised recently by Jordi Fernández.

On Wednesday, the Nets got to match up with another tanking rival. The Bulls also leapfrogged them in the lottery standings and jumped up to fourth, taking Caleb Wilson, whom Brooklyn also reportedly coveted.

Wilson came into Wednesday inconsistent but being allowed — encouraged? — to play through his mistakes. He was averaging 18.9 points, 6.2 rebounds and several highlight plays in 30.8 minutes.

#2746. Is a bottom in for the Nasdaq-100? Charts to watch

(See the video above for Frank's complete chart breakdown.)

Is the Nasdaq-100's recent bounce a sign that the bottom is in? We're going to look at several charts to help answer that question.

First, let's remember how we got here. In September, the NDX broke out from a bullish cup-and-handle pattern, producing a 33,200-upside target. That breakout quickly failed, however, and gave way to a bearish pattern that broke down aggressively two weeks ago.

The decline brought the index relatively close to its 26,350 downside target before the current rebound began.

Zooming out, it's telling to see where the bounce originated. Three important forms of support converged in the 25,000-26,000 area:

This confluence of support helped encourage buying after a roughly 15% decline.

For perspective, we also see what larger drawdowns of 20%, 30%, 40%, and 50% would look like … a lot worse.

The following chart tracks NDX drawdowns from 52-week highs going back to just after the financial crisis. Only a handful of declines exceeded 20%, and three produced relatively quick reversals: late 2018, the Covid lows in 2020 and April 2025.

Historically, buying into declines of approximately 15%–25% has generally paid off, even when additional downside occurred first (yellow highlights).

The chart also highlights previous declines of 10%–16% in green, putting the current pullback into perspective.

The major exception was 2022, when the NDX eventually declined nearly 36% over approximately 10 months ... a much worse outcome, which many investors are concerned could happen again now.

That raises the key question: Are we experiencing another routine correction, or the early stages of a larger bear market?

One important clue will be how far this bounce progresses.

Any rally that fails to reclaim the previous highs could establish a significant lower high. Additional lower highs would provide stronger evidence of a developing, longer downtrend.

We saw this in March 2022, when that first sharp rebound effort failed to reach the previous high before a much more severe decline followed.

The bottom line: The current bounce is encouraging, particularly given where it originated and knowing how well buying prior 10-20% drawdowns has paid off.

From here, it's all about the follow through.  We don't need to see new highs right away, but any rally from here that's met with another wave of strong selling could reignite downside momentum.

#2745. Musk accuses Zelenskyy of lying about Starshield restrictions in Ukraine

SpaceX founder Elon Musk accused Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of being untruthful about restrictions around Ukraine's Starshield network and said Kyiv wanted to use Starlink for offensive operations.

Asked at The New York Times' Dealbook Summit about Zelenskyy's claims that Starshield had been slowed down, Musk said, "That's false ... I don't want to blow your mind, but Zelenskyy is not always truthful."

When pressed on whether he meant Ukraine was not always truthful, Musk doubled down with a reply: "No, it's not always truthful."

His comments came after Zelenskyy on Wednesday said speed restrictions remained in place on Starshield, hampering Ukraine's ability to intercept Russian missile and drone strikes. "We are discussing this with the American side," he said.

Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, stoking a conflict that has resulted in a refugee crisis and hundreds of thousands of deaths. Ukraine has been able to beat back Russian forces more effectively than many observers thought possible, despite having a much smaller land area and population.

However, it relies heavily on SpaceX's Starlink and Starshield for capabilities like battlefield communications and drone operations. Musk has previously said that "if we were to turn off Starlink, the entire Ukrainian front would collapse immediately."

The SpaceX CEO sought to distinguish between Starlink, a commercial satellite network, and Starshield, a military system developed by SpaceX and operated by the U.S. government.

Musk said that Starlink is subject to speed limits because it is not intended for offensive military operations, adding that such missions should instead use the Starshield network.

"Any action taken by Starshield is up to the War Department. Starlink is commercial and is not intended as a weapon of war," Musk said, referring to the U.S. Department of Defense.

In October, Musk said the U.S. government and President Donald Trump were responsible for any restrictions on Ukraine's Starshield network after slowdowns to the service were reported.

"Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," Musk wrote on X.

The Wall Street Journal later reported on Oct. 20 that Musk had ordered the slowdown, citing U.S. officials and people familiar with the matter.

"What I'm trying to tell you is Zelenskyy is actually asking to use the Starlink commercial satellites for events of military actions, and we have declined to do so, as we have declined to do so from the beginning of this conflict," Musk added in the interview.

On Oct. 24, Musk said SpaceX had restricted Ukraine's access to Starlink because Kyiv had violated the service's terms by using it for offensive drone strikes, a claim Ukrainian officials disputed.

"Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week," Musk wrote on X one day after.

CNBC has reached out to Ukraine's ministry of foreign affairs for comment but did not receive a response. The president's office could not immediately be reached.

#2743. RJ Luis looks as advertised in LSU basketball win - after signing NBA deal

RJ Luis is officially back in college basketball. He certainly looked a level above the rest at times, as expected.

The LSU guard, who received a preliminary injunction on Friday, Nov. 13, checked into the game for the first time this season against Louisiana-Monroe on Nov. 18, adding a new wrinkle to his ongoing eligibility saga. He subbed in with 2:29 left in the first half, playing the remainder of the period before the Warhawks took a 39-34 lead into halftime.

In just 15 minutes off the bench a day after he was officially added to LSU's roster, the former St. John's star and NBA contract signee scored 11 points with nine rebounds, an assist and a block in the 79-67 win over Louisiana-Monroe. His 15 minutes were the second fewest for the Tigers in the game, but his 11 points were the fourth-most among nine players.

REQUIRED READING: As LSU rosters RJ Luis, Georgia AG encourages SEC to punish university - severely

Luis signed both a two-way contract and an Exhibit 10 deal with the Utah Jazz and Boston Celtics, although he never played in a regular season NBA game after going undrafted in the 2025 NBA Draft. His strong play for LSU off the bench will undoubtably spark even more controversy, especially given his journey back to college basketball.

LSU coach Will Wade didn't elaborate on his decision to play Luis after the game.

"I'm going to refer to our university's statement from yesterday," he said. "I'll be happy to answer any questions about how he played, but going to refer in terms of anything about his eligibility and rostering him to the university's statement yesterday.

"Everybody who played tonight is eligible."

The 2025 Big East Player of the Year at St. John's is a huge pickup for the Tigers, particularly if he's ruled eligible for the remainder of the season. He was officially added to LSU's roster on Nov. 17 in a move that drew concerns from the SEC and outside forces, such as the attorney general of Georgia, who wrote a letter about Luis' eligibility to SEC commissioner Greg Sankey on Nov. 18.

Luis' preliminary injunction included terms that barred Luis and LSU from being punished for him playing in games. The SEC won't seek punishment for LSU adding Luis to its roster, despite not supporting the move.

"This is a deeply concerning and disappointing development," the conference wrote in a statement on Nov. 17. "The conference will continue to uphold and defend the standards and policies established by its member universities."

The SEC adopted rules this offseason that ban players that have signed an NBA contract or did not properly withdraw from the NBA draft. Luis' attorneys have maintained the stance that since he never appeared in a regular season game, he was never a professional, despite appearing to be included in the SEC's new rules.

It's unclear if this is the end of Luis' eligibility saga, although it doesn't appear the SEC will seek any further action against the standout guard.

Luis averaged 18.2 points with 7.2 rebounds in his last season of college basketball in 2024-25. He started his career at UMass in 2022-23, leaving college early for the NBA draft as a junior.

#2742. Anthropic IPO raises over $81 billion in largest offering on record, topping SpaceX

Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 per share on Wednesday, above the expected range, setting the stage for the Claude creator's eagerly awaited Nasdaq listing and a historic moment for the artificial intelligence industry.

The company, along with its seven co-founders, upsized the offering, selling about 980 million shares, according to a press release. That brings the amount raised to $81.3 billion, surpassing SpaceX, which held a record IPO in June. Elon Musk's company raised $75 billion initially and a total of $85.7 billion after underwriters exercised their overallotment.

Anthropic's fully diluted market cap sits at around $1.5 trillion. The stock is expected to begin trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker symbol "ANT."

The listing is a major test for the AI industry, which has experienced a set of recent shocks, including a dramatic backlash that was felt at the polls in the midterm elections and last week's ouster of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The market was already jittery on concerns that rising interest rates will make debt unaffordable for many data center developers and neoclouds.

After publicly unveiling its prospectus in October, Anthropic updated the document last week with an expected price range between $70 and $78 per share.  The company had been planning to sell 825 million shares.

Tech's biggest companies have significant exposure to Anthropic, as an investor, partner or customer. Amazon and Google both own stakes valued at over $100 billion, and a group of tech companies, including Google, Microsoft, Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices agreed to collectively invest $26 billion at the IPO price. Anthropic, meanwhile, is a buyer of costly systems from Nvidia, Google, Amazon and AMD.

"I think if we do this right, we can create an age of miracles where humanity is able to solve problems that have eluded us for millennia," Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said in Anthropic's roadshow video. "We have to make sure that all the risks, all the ways that things can go wrong with this technology, we very carefully address those risks as we bring the benefits and as we have a viable business at the same time."

Amodei co-founded Anthropic in 2021 alongside a handful of other researchers less than six years ago, after the group collectively defected from OpenAI. The company is best known for developing a family of AI models called Claude, and it primarily sells its products and services to other businesses.

According to the latest prospectus, each co-founder is selling 3.38 million shares for total proceeds of $1.96 billion.

Anthropic has been racing to maintain an edge over OpenAI and Google in the enterprise market, and it experienced a period of explosive growth in 2026, driven largely by the popularity of its AI coding tool, Claude Code. OpenAI has confidentially filed for an IPO and has said a debut is likely in 2027.

For the nine months ended Sept. 30, Anthropic said, it generated $33.24 billion in revenue, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year, according to its prospectus. The company reported a $104 billion net loss during the nine-month period, though most of that was due to the change in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Anthropic lost $25.1 billion over the same stretch in 2025, the filing said.

Anthropic said in an amended filing that its run-rate revenue was roughly $81 billion at the end of October, up $10 billion from the previous month.

The company has faced plenty of challenges during its meteoric rise over its positions on safety, regulation and national security, leading to two high-profile disputes with the U.S. government this year. Its prospectus included more than 90 pages of risk factors for investors to consider ahead of its IPO.

"Our aim is to help humankind chart a safe course through this technological evolution, open new frontiers of discovery, and bring forth an age of miracles," Anthropic's co-founders wrote in the company's prospectus. "Everyone who owns our stock, whether an institution or an individual, becomes part of that effort."

#2741. Cameron vs Mayer 2 Leads Boxing Schedule Additions

A flurry of fight matchups have been added to the boxing schedule through the end of 2026 and early in 2027.

Leading the list is the rematch between unified super welterweight champion Chantelle Cameron and pound-for-pound former champion Mikaela Mayer

Minimumweight world champion Oscar Collazo will fight in the co-main event of Amanda Serrano's farewell fight in Puerto Rico.

With just a few weeks to go until boxing media will put together their year-end awards for 2026, additional fight matchups are being announced and added to the calendar in 2026, along with cards to look forward to in early 2027.

Most Valuable Promotions (MVP) announced the rematch between number two Ring pound-for-pound boxer, two-division world champion and reigning unified WBO, WBA, and WBC Super Welterweight world champion Chantelle Cameron of England (23-1, 8 KOs) and fifth Ring pound-for-pound, three-division world champion, and reigning WBO World Welterweight champion Mikaela Mayer of Colorado Springs (22-3, 5 KOs).

Cameron vs Mayer 2 has been added as the co-main event of MVP's Jake Paul vs. Cédric Doumbé Christmas Eve card on December 24 at Coca-Cola Arena in Dubai, UAE.

If you don't think this one will be spicy, let us remind you how the first fight went down between Cameron and Mayer.

Cameron earned a unanimous decision over Mayer in August at MVPW06 in Birmingham, England, where Cameron claimed Mayer's WBA and WBC titles and unified three world championships. Mayer immediately called for a rematch, and now the showdown is booked.

Cameron enters determined to defend her unified crown and cement her place among boxing's pound-for-pound elite, while Mayer looks to avenge her defeat and reclaim the titles she lost just four months earlier.

Chantelle "Il Capo" Cameron is one of the most recognized names in women's boxing. Cameron won the vacant WBC super lightweight world title in October 2020 before winning the IBF and Ring Magazine titles, then the WBA title, to become undisputed champion. Cameron successfully defended her titles against Katie Taylor in May 2023, the only professional to beat Taylor in her career, before a November 2023 rematch resulted in an MD for Taylor.

Cameron won the WBC interim super lightweight title in her next fight, defended it twice successfully, then stepped up to win the vacant WBO World Super Welterweight title in April 2026 on MVPW01.

"I am genuinely excited to box in one of my favorite places on December 24 in Dubai," said Cameron. "I cannot thank Jake, Nakisa and Mike enough for this opportunity to box on a huge show. They promised to keep me active in 2026, and my third fight in nine months proves just that. We agreed to the rematch before the first fight, so we both kept our word, and now the rematch is on the biggest stage in boxing."

Three-division champion and reigning WBO World Welterweight champion Mikaela Mayer jumped out to a 17-0 record to begin her pro career while winning a pair of super featherweight world titles and becoming a pound-for-pound mainstay.

In January 2024, she contended for the IBF welterweight world title against Natasha Jonas, then seized her second opportunity to become a two-weight world champion in September 2024, defeating WBO World Welterweight Sandy Ryan in a Fight of the Year contender before besting her again in a rematch.

Mayer became a three-division champion with a defeat of Mary Spencer in October 2025 to win the WBA, WBC, and WBO super welterweight titles.

"Mayer vs. Cameron was a great fight that I truly hope everyone enjoyed. Although I don't feel I performed to my highest potential, I've been working hard to fix the mistakes I made and I will 100% come back stronger! I'm taking my belts back on December 24," said Mayer.

Oscar Collazo is among Puerto Rico's most popular young champions. Photo: Golden Boy Boxing

Most Valuable Promotions (MVP) confirmed an additional world championship matchup for The Last Walk: Amanda Serrano vs. Skye Falzon on Saturday, January 9 at Coliseo de Puerto Rico in San Juan.

Puerto Rico's undefeated pound-for-pound star and reigning WBA and Ring Magazine minimumweight world champion Oscar Collazo (15-0, 12 KOs) will defend his titles against top-ranked Filipino challenger Joey Canoy (26-5-2, 15 KOs) in the 12-round co-main event at 105lbs.

Also added is MVP's undefeated featherweight contender Jan Paul Rivera (17-0, 7 KOs) in a 10-round bout against a to-be-announced opponent.

Shurretta Metcalf and Krystal Rosado have a lot to gain with a win. Photo: Most Valuable Promotions

Former IBF world champion Shurretta Metcalf (15-6-1, 2 KOs) will also return in an eight-round bantamweight rematch against MVP's rising contender and Amanda Serrano protege Krystal Rosado (10-1, 2 KOs), who seeks redemption after Metcalf handed Rosado her first professional defeat in October 2025.

Nakisa Bidarian and Jake Paul, Founders of Most Valuable Promotions, said: "Amanda Serrano's final fight deserves a card worthy of her extraordinary legacy, and we're delivering back-to-back championship fights alongside some of boxing's most compelling rising talent."

Oscar Collazo first captured the WBO World Minimumweight title in 2023, becoming the fastest Puerto Rican fighter to win a world championship in just seven professional bouts. He unified titles by winning the WBA belt in November 2024 and the division's first-ever Ring Magazine title. After successfully defending titles, "El Pupilo" moved up two weight classes and earned a knockout victory to win the WBO International flyweight title.

His opponent, Joey "The Babyface" Canoy is an experienced southpaw from the Philippines. The former WBC International minimumweight champion, Canoy is currently ranked second by the WBC, sixth by the WBO, WBA and Ring Magazine, and thirteenth by the IBF. He will make his U.S. debut against Collazo.

"It is a privilege for me to be part of this very special event, where we will have the chance to support our champion, Amanda Serrano, on a historic night — her farewell to boxing — taking place in front of her own people at the Coliseo de Puerto Rico," said Collazo. It is an honor to share this moment with her and to be part of a fight card that is so significant for our sport and for Puerto Rico.

"On Saturday, January 9th, we are going to leave everything in the ring and give Puerto Rico an unforgettable night! Amanda, count on me to celebrate this very special night together! Puerto Rico, I'll see you at the 'Choli'!"

Light heavyweight contender Iman Khataev and his friends will return to the ring on January 28 in Montreal. Photo: Eye of the Tiger Management

Eye of the Tiger Management's 2027 season gets underway on January 28 at the Casino de Montréal with Olympic medalist and NABF light heavyweight titlist Imam Khataev (13-1, 12 KOs) appearing in his first main event after three co-main event appearances.

The Tokyo 2020 Games bronze medal winner Khataev picked up the NABF title in January 2024 by stopping Polish champion Michael Ludwiczak in the second round. He went on to put four wins on his record before taking on David Morrell Jr., scoring the first knockdown against the highly regarded Cuban before having to settle for a split-decision loss in a highly controversial verdict.

Khataev has since put another trio of wins on his resume. Khataev is ranked third by the IBF and WBC, and sixth by the WBO in a highly competitive division. Khataev hopes to earn a world championship opportunity with a win on January 28. His opponent will be named at a future date.

Also appearing on the card are super middleweight Moreno Fendero of France, light heavyweight Mehmet Unal, Canadian Olympic medalist Wyatt Sanford, and newly signed Keven Beausejour, all undefeated.

#2740. 2027 UFL Draft tracker, results, top prospects as Diego Pavia finds landing spot

The 2027 UFL Draft has arrived, and football fans have one question on their minds heading into the event. Where will former Vanderbilt quarterback Diego Pavia land?

Pavia announced in October he was planning to join the UFL ahead of its 2027 season. The 2025 Heisman Trophy runner-up will instantly become one of the spring football league's biggest stars and will look to prove to all the teams that passed on him in the 2026 NFL Draft that he deserves a chance to play professionally.

While Pavia is the marquee name in the 2027 UFL Draft's player pool, there are plenty of other players with whom football fans will be familiar. A total of 120 players will be selected across the two-day, 15-round event that will help fill out the rosters of the UFL's eight current teams.

Of course, not every player selected is guaranteed to play in the UFL. The spring football draft is a rights draft, meaning teams retain the rights to negotiate with selected players should they choose to play in the UFL.

Still, spring football fans will be eager to see the crop of talent that could be poised to enter the UFL ahead of its 2027 season.

USA TODAY Sports is tracking the results of the 2027 UFL Draft. Follow along with the latest picks and a breakdown of the top prospects available in this year's draft class.

Pavia starred across two seasons at Vanderbilt, leading the Commodores to a winning record in back-to-back seasons. That included a 10-3 mark in 2025, a season during which he completed 70.6% of his passes for 3,539 yards, 29 touchdowns and eight interceptions while adding 862 yards and 10 touchdowns on the ground.

Pavia finished as the runner-up in the 2025 Heisman Trophy voting and signed with the Baltimore Ravens after going undrafted in the 2026 NFL Draft. He was released before the preseason and now will look for a shot to play in the UFL.

Martinez played spring football in 2024, when he won the USFL MVP while a member of the Birmingham Stallions after throwing for 1,748 yards, 15 touchdowns and three interceptions while adding a league-high 528 rushing yards and three scores on the ground. He parlayed that opportunity into a chance with the New York Jets and has spent the last three NFL seasons with the Jets, San Francisco 49ers and Seattle Seahawks.

Currently, Martinez is on the Seahawks' practice squad. It isn't clear whether the 26-year-old will look to return to spring football, but his dual-threat ability will certainly make him a hot commodity should he decide to do so.

Steele went undrafted out of UCLA in 2024 but quickly earned a role in the Kansas City Chiefs' backfield. He totaled 183 yards on 56 carries as a rookie but has only handled one touch, a 4-yard reception, over his last two years with the Chiefs and the Philadelphia Eagles.

Steele (6-0, 228 pounds) is a big-bodied bruiser who runs with great physicality. That could make the 24-year-old a goal-line hammer at the UFL level.

Floriea may not be a household name, but he endeared himself to Cleveland Browns fans during the 2025 and 2026 preseasons. The Kent State product notched a combined seven receptions for 125 yards and three touchdowns across four games of preseason action with the Browns.

Floriea spent the 2025 season on Cleveland's practice squad but failed to earn a spot despite a strong performance in the 2026 preseason. The 25-year-old is small at 5-8, 180 pounds, but his hands and separation skills could make him a quality UFL pass-catcher.

Cunningham, a former Louisville quarterback, began his career as a signal-caller for the Baltimore Ravens and New England Patriots. However, in recent seasons, he transitioned to the receiver position and played one game at the position for the Detroit Lions.

Cunningham, 28, has never attempt a pass nor made a catch at the NFL level, but his dual-threat skill set would make him an intriguing fit for the UFL.

Cunningham isn't the only Louisville product who could draw interest in the UFL draft. Thrash, a 2024 fifth-round pick by the Browns, is in the player pool, and UFL teams would love to get their hands on the speedy 6-0, 190-pound receiver.

Thrash recorded 13 receptions for 129 yards across two seasons with the Browns. He also spent two weeks on the Las Vegas Raiders' practice squad during the 2026 NFL season.

Bell was a seventh-round pick by the Patriots in the 2024 NFL Draft after he enjoyed a standout career at South Carolina and Florida State. Bell made just two catches for 20 yards with the Patriots, but he showed off his upside as a senior with the Seminoles, recording 39 receptions for 503 yards and two touchdowns.

Bell is a bit short for a tight end at 6-2, 241 pounds, but he has a well-rounded skill set that could make him hard to cover for UFL defenders.

Wright's name will be familiar to college football fans, as he tried to become one of the first players to see action with an NFL team and return to the college level. His efforts were denied, leaving Wright in limbo after the Browns waived him and LSU chose not to add him to its roster.

Wright (6-4, 246 pounds) may yet get a chance to play professionally in the UFL. The Ole Miss product had 39 catches for 635 yards and five touchdowns his final season with the Rebels and it's easy to see him developing into a mismatch threat in the spring game.

Pete, like Wright, made headlines during the 2026 NFL preseason. The Kentucky product spent time with the Dallas Cowboys, becoming the first NFL player from the Navajo Nation and earning rave reviews for a locker room speech following Dallas' preseason win over the Arizona Cardinals.

At 6-9, 309 pounds, Pete looks the part of a high-upside, developmental offensive lineman. Developing in the UFL could help him eventually emerge as a contributor thanks to his size alone.

Martin-Rhodes is one of the highest-drafted former NFL players in the 2027 UFL Draft's player pool. He was a third-round pick by the Lions in 2023 but was never quite able to carve out a role during his NFL stops with the Lions and Pittsburgh Steelers.

Martin-Rhodes has just six career tackles and no sacks. The 27-year-old will look to show off his abilities as a run stuffer behind his 6-5, 330-pound frame.

#2739. Celtics announce starting lineup against Denver Nuggets

DENVER — The Celtics will start Derrick White, Jordan Walsh, Paul George, Jayson Tatum, and Neemias Queta when they face the Denver Nuggets on Wednesday.

Queta is coming off his first rest night of the season, a Monday night Celtics loss to the Orlando Magic, which snapped the team's 6-game win streak. The Celtics struggled without him, with Luka Garza starting and Mitchell Robinson and Chris Cenac Jr. playing backup minutes.

But, Monday was more of an anomaly than a typical Boston performance; the Celtics have the fourth-best offensive rating and second-best defensive rating in the league. Only the Minnesota Timberwolves (104.0) have a better defensive rating than Boston (106.1).

And, before tip-off, Nuggets head coach David Adelman praised the Celtics' defensive versatility.

"I think it's been the most underrated thing about them," Adelman said. "Queta is a very active big…Obviously Derrick's always been a good defender. All those guys, they bought into what they do."

Adelman also said he thought people overlooked how good the Celtics might be this season after Jaylen Brown was traded to the Philadelphia 76ers in exchange for Paul George and draft compensation.

"I thought quietly what was maybe misunderstood was: everybody else is coming back. Tatum was back, all that shooting's back. It's not like Pritchard's in the trade, and there's a lot of really good players. Jaylen Brown's an all-time great player, but their team core is back."

The Celtics are 11-3 entering the season; the Nuggets are 7-5.

The Nuggets will start Jamal Murray, Christian Braun, Cam Johnson, Aaron Gordon, and Nikola Jokic.

Pregame, Joe Mazzulla was asked about limiting Nikola Jokic — and explained there's no easy way to do it.

"You have to defend them with your offense," Mazzulla said. "You can't play inefficient offense. You can't allow them to get more shots than you. You can't turn the ball over. If you get into a close game, you have to pick your poison. He is a very good player, and he has the ability to put pressure on every single coverage. He's seen every single coverage. So it's not about stopping him. It's about containing him and winning on the margins. We can't put him on the free throw line. You can't give up offensive rebounds. You can't give up back cuts, and you have to play efficient offense. Guys like that test the margins, and you have to play two-way basketball. You have to be able to attack them so that you can defend them. And you wouldn't guard them the same way down five as you would tied, as you would up five, because of their ability to put stress on multiple coverages. So you have to play well-balanced basketball against a team like this tonight, and the margins are super important. You start giving up back cuts, offensive rebounds, fouls; you're not going to be able to guard them in the half-court, so you've got to be disciplined on both ends of the floor."
